cards.q: How do you distinguish a **macule** from a **patch**?
cards.a:
• Both are **flat** lesions with a change in colour/texture – not raised or depressed
• **Macule: <10 mm** (e.g. freckles, early chickenpox spots)
• **Patch: >10 mm** (e.g. vitiligo, melasma)
cards.m: Same flatness, different size – a patch is just a big macule.

cards.q: What separates a **vesicle** from a **bulla**, and give a classic example of each?
cards.a:
• Both are raised, **fluid-filled blisters**
• **Vesicle: <5 mm** – chickenpox, herpes simplex
• **Bulla: >5 mm** – bullous pemphigoid
cards.m: Vesicle = little vessel of fluid; bulla = big bubble.

cards.q: Define a **pustule** and name two common causes.
cards.a:
• A raised lesion filled with **pus**
• Examples: **acne vulgaris**, **folliculitis**
• Varicella vesicles also evolve into pustules before crusting

cards.q: How does a **papule** differ from a **nodule**?
cards.a:
• **Papule:** raised, palpable, **<5 mm** – acne, insect bite, wart
• **Nodule:** raised, palpable, **>5 mm**, extends into the **dermis or subcutaneous tissue** – lipoma, dermatofibroma
cards.m: Nodule = deeper and bigger; feel it, don’t just see it.

cards.q: What is a **plaque**, and which two common conditions produce plaques?
cards.a:
• A **palpable**, flat-topped lesion of large diameter, raised (or depressed) relative to surrounding skin
• Slide uses **>20 mm**; many texts use >10 mm – the key is a broad, plateau-like lesion
• Examples: **psoriasis**, **tinea corporis**
cards.m: Plaque = plateau.

cards.q: Describe a **wheal** and its typical causes.
cards.a:
• Elevated, **pruritic**, red/pale lesion caused by **localised dermal oedema**
• **Transient** – individual wheals usually fade within 24 hours
• Causes: **urticaria**, insect bites
cards.m: Wheal comes and goes like a wave – here today, gone tomorrow.

cards.q: **Scaling** vs **crust** – what is the difference?
cards.a:
• **Scale:** heaped-up accumulation of dead epithelium (**stratum corneum**) on the surface
• **Crust:** **dried exudate** – serous, purulent or haemorrhagic
• Chickenpox lesions end as **crusts**, not scales
cards.m: Scale = dead skin; crust = dried juice.

cards.q: What is **lichenification** and what causes it?
cards.a:
• **Thickening of the skin** with **accentuated normal skin markings**
• Caused by **repeated scratching or rubbing**
• Classic in **chronic eczema** (itch–scratch cycle)
cards.m: Looks like tree-bark lichen – rubbed so often the skin toughens.

cards.q: **Nummular** vs **annular** configuration – how do they differ, with examples?
cards.a:
• **Nummular:** **coin-shaped**, uniformly involved disc – nummular (discoid) eczema
• **Annular:** **ring** with **central clearing** and active edge – tinea corporis
cards.m: Nummular = full coin; annular = ring with a hole.

cards.q: What do **gyrate** and **linear** configurations suggest?
cards.a:
• **Gyrate:** reddish **curvilinear/wavy** or annular lesions – e.g. **erythema annulare centrifugum**
• **Linear:** straight lines – suggests **excoriations from scratching** or an external cause
cards.m: Gyrate = gyrus-like swirls on the skin.

cards.q: **Erythema** vs **purpura** – mechanism and bedside test?
cards.a:
• **Erythema:** **capillary dilatation**/increased dermal blood flow → **blanches** on pressure
• **Purpura:** **haemorrhage** from small vessels into skin → **does not blanch**
• Test by pressing with a clear glass (**glass/tumbler test**) or finger
cards.m: Blood in the vessel blanches; blood out of the vessel stays.

cards.q: Define **erythroderma** and its main causes.
cards.a:
• Widespread reddening of **>90%** of the skin surface
• Due to inflammatory skin disease – **psoriasis, eczema**, drug reactions
• Risks: fluid/heat loss, hypothermia, infection → usually needs referral
• Note: slide says 'psoriasis/edema'; it should read **eczema**
cards.m: Erythroderma = 'red all over'.

cards.q: How are **petechiae, purpura and ecchymoses** distinguished?
cards.a:
• All are **non-blanching** bleeding into the skin
• **Petechiae:** pinpoint, **<2 mm**
• **Purpura:** **2–10 mm**
• **Ecchymosis:** **>10 mm** (bruise)
• Fever + petechiae/purpura = **meningococcaemia until proven otherwise**; also dengue
cards.m: Pin → coin → bruise as size grows.

cards.q: How are the differential diagnoses of **fever with rash** grouped in this seminar?
cards.a:
• **Viral:** varicella, measles, roseola, HFMD, dengue
• **Bacterial/rickettsial:** typhoid, typhus, scarlet fever, toxic shock syndrome, meningococcaemia
• **Drug-related/immune-mediated:** Stevens-Johnson syndrome/TEN
• **Inflammatory/unknown:** Kawasaki disease
cards.m: Bugs (viral, bacterial), drugs, and the mystery vasculitis.

cards.q: What causes **varicella**, and how does it lead to shingles later?
cards.a:
• **Varicella-zoster virus (VZV, HHV-3)** – primary systemic infection
• Virus becomes **latent in dorsal root (sensory) ganglia**
• **Reactivation** → **herpes zoster (shingles)** in a dermatome
cards.m: Chickenpox moves in, sleeps in the ganglia, wakes up as shingles.

cards.q: How is **varicella transmitted**?
cards.a:
• **Airborne droplets**
• **Direct contact with vesicular fluid**
• Possibly respiratory secretions and fomites
• **Highly contagious** – most susceptible household contacts become infected

cards.q: What is the **incubation period** of varicella?
cards.a:
• Range **10–21 days**
• Average **14–15 days**
• Hence exposed contacts are watched for up to 21 days (28 days if VZIG given – pearl)
cards.m: About two weeks – 'chickenpox fortnight'.

cards.q: When is a patient with varicella **infectious**?
cards.a:
• From about **1–2 days before rash onset** (slide: 2 days)
• **Until all lesions have crusted**
• Crusted lesions are not infectious
cards.m: Starts before you see it; ends when every spot is a scab.

cards.q: Describe the **evolution of the varicella rash**.
cards.a:
• **Macule → papule → clear vesicle → pustule → crust**
• Vesicles: 'dewdrop on a rose petal'
• Appears in **crops**, so lesions at **different stages** coexist
• **Intensely pruritic**; may involve oral, oropharyngeal and genital mucosa
cards.m: Crops = a garden with seedlings, flowers and dead heads at once (unlike smallpox, all same stage).

cards.q: What is the **distribution** of the varicella rash in an unvaccinated person?
cards.a:
• **Centripetal** – densest on **chest and back**
• Starts on chest, back and face, then spreads to the rest of the body
• Fewer lesions on distal limbs
• Contrast: smallpox is **centrifugal** (face and extremities, palms/soles)
cards.m: Centripetal = towards the centre (trunk).

cards.q: How does the **prodrome** of varicella differ between children and adults?
cards.a:
• Prodrome ~**24 hours before rash**: fever, malaise, lethargy, headache, anorexia
• **Children:** often **no prodrome** – rash is the first sign
• **Adults:** prodrome usual, and illness is more severe
cards.m: Kids skip the trailer; adults get the full movie.

cards.q: What is **breakthrough varicella** and how does it present?
cards.a:
• Wild-type VZV infection **>42 days after vaccination**
• **Mild**: afebrile or low-grade fever, usually **<50 lesions**
• Mainly **maculopapular** (few vesicles), shorter illness
• **25–30%** of one-dose recipients with breakthrough disease look like unvaccinated cases
• Still contagious
cards.m: Vaccinated kids get 'chickenpox-lite'.

cards.q: How is varicella **diagnosed**, and when is a test needed?
cards.a:
• It is a **clinical diagnosis**
• Tests only if atypical, immunocompromised, pregnant or severe: **PCR of vesicle fluid** (most sensitive) or VZV serology for immune status

cards.q: List the **non-pharmacological** measures for chickenpox.
cards.a:
• **Rest and isolation**
• Keep **well hydrated**
• **Cool baths** with baking soda or colloidal/uncooked oatmeal
• **Trim fingernails**, minimise scratching (prevents infection and scars)
• Good hygiene, loose comfortable clothing

cards.q: What symptomatic **drugs** are used in uncomplicated childhood varicella?
cards.a:
• **Itch:** calamine lotion + oral **antihistamine**
• **Fever:** **paracetamol**
• Antiviral therapy is **not routinely indicated** in healthy children

cards.q: Why must **aspirin** (and ideally NSAIDs) be avoided in varicella?
cards.a:
• **Aspirin → Reye syndrome**: acute encephalopathy + fatty liver failure in children with viral illness (varicella, influenza)
• **NSAIDs** (e.g. ibuprofen) are linked with severe **invasive group A streptococcal** skin/soft-tissue infection in varicella
• Use **paracetamol** instead
cards.m: Pox + aspirin = Reye; pox + ibuprofen = flesh-eating strep risk.

cards.q: Which varicella patients should receive **oral antivirals**?
cards.a:
• **Adolescents (≥13 years) and adults** – more severe disease
• **Pregnant** women, **smokers**, chronic lung or skin disease, long-term steroid/salicylate use
• **Immunocompromised** and neonates → usually **IV aciclovir** via hospital
• Healthy children: symptomatic care only
cards.m: Big kids, adults, bumps (pregnancy) and broken immunity.

cards.q: Give the **antiviral regimen and timing** for adult varicella.
cards.a:
• **Aciclovir 800 mg five times daily for 7 days** (or valaciclovir 1 g three times daily)
• Best **within 24 hours of rash onset**; slide: within 24–48 h of new vesicles appearing
• **>48 h** after rash onset with **no new lesions** → symptomatic treatment only
• Reduces severity and duration

cards.q: What is the **most common complication** of varicella in children?
cards.a:
• **Secondary bacterial infection** of skin lesions – **Staphylococcus aureus** or **Streptococcus pyogenes** (impetigo, cellulitis)
• Can leave **pitted scars**
• Rarely invasive GAS → necrotising fasciitis or toxic shock

cards.q: What is the most important serious complication of varicella in **adults**, and its red flags?
cards.a:
• **Varicella pneumonia** – higher risk in **smokers, pregnancy**, immunocompromised
• Usually 1–6 days after rash onset
• Red flags: **cough, breathlessness, chest pain, tachypnoea, hypoxia, haemoptysis**
• → **Urgent hospital referral** for IV aciclovir
cards.m: Adult with pox and breathless = pneumonia until proven otherwise.

cards.q: Name the **neurological complications** of varicella.
cards.a:
• **Acute cerebellar ataxia** – commonest in children, ~1 week after rash, usually benign and self-limiting
• **Encephalitis** – drowsiness, seizures (serious)
• Meningitis
• Reye syndrome if aspirin given
cards.m: Wobbly but alert = cerebellitis; drowsy and fitting = encephalitis.

cards.q: Which varicella complications need **urgent referral to hospital**?
cards.a:
• **Disseminated varicella** (immunocompromised)
• **Varicella pneumonia** / ARDS
• **Varicella encephalitis**
• **Reye syndrome**
• **Neonatal varicella** and congenital varicella syndrome

cards.q: What are the risks of **varicella in pregnancy**?
cards.a:
• **Mother:** severe **varicella pneumonia**
• **Fetus <20 weeks:** **congenital varicella syndrome** (~1–2%) – limb hypoplasia, cicatricial skin scarring, eye and brain defects
• **Neonate:** severe **neonatal varicella** if maternal rash **5 days before to 2 days after delivery**
• Non-immune exposed pregnant women → **VZIG**

cards.q: What is the **varicella vaccination** schedule on the slides, and its main contraindications?
cards.a:
• **Two doses: 12–15 months and 4–6 years** (CDC schedule); can be given to susceptible older children and adults
• **>90% effective** at preventing severe disease
• In Malaysia it is **not in the national schedule** – optional (private)
• **Live vaccine** → contraindicated in **pregnancy** and immunosuppression

cards.q: What **post-exposure prophylaxis** is available for varicella?
cards.a:
• **Varicella vaccine within 3–5 days** of exposure – healthy, non-immune, non-pregnant contacts
• **VZIG** for **high-risk** groups: immunocompromised, **non-immune pregnant women**, newborns – ideally ASAP (within 10 days)
cards.m: Healthy → vaccine; high-risk → immunoglobulin.

cards.q: What **isolation** advice do you give for chickenpox?
cards.a:
• Isolate **until all lesions have crusted** (usually ~5–7 days after onset)
• Avoid contact with **pregnant women, newborns and immunocompromised** people
• Keep off school/childcare until crusted

cards.q: What virus causes **measles**?
cards.a:
• **Measles virus** – an RNA virus of the genus **Morbillivirus**, family **Paramyxoviridae**
• Commonest in children
• Humans are the only reservoir – hence elimination is possible

cards.q: How is measles transmitted, and how infectious is it?
cards.a:
• **Direct contact with infectious droplets**
• **Airborne spread** when an infected person breathes, coughs or sneezes – virus lingers in room air
• One of the **most contagious** diseases (R0 ~12–18)
• Infectious from **4 days before to 4 days after rash onset** (pearl)
cards.m: Measles: 4 days either side of the rash.

cards.q: What is the **clinical case definition** of measles used for notification?
cards.a:
Any person with:
• **Fever**, AND
• **Maculopapular rash**, AND
• **Cough OR coryza OR conjunctivitis**
cards.m: Fever + rash + one of the 3 Cs.

cards.q: What are the **risk factors** for measles and severe measles?
cards.a:
• **Immunosuppression**
• **Unvaccinated** people, including travellers to endemic areas
• **Malnourished children**, especially **vitamin A deficient**

cards.q: Describe the **prodromal stage** of measles.
cards.a:
• Lasts **2–4 days**
• **Fever** + the **3 Cs: cough, coryza, conjunctivitis**
• **Koplik spots** appear on the buccal mucosa near the end of the prodrome
• Child is miserable and unwell
cards.m: 3 Cs + K: Cough, Coryza, Conjunctivitis + Koplik.

cards.q: What are **Koplik spots** and why are they useful?
cards.a:
• Tiny **white spots like grains of salt** on a red **buccal mucosa** (opposite the lower molars)
• **Pathognomonic** of measles
• Appear **before the rash** and fade as the rash spreads – so look early
cards.m: Salt grains on a red tablecloth.

cards.q: Describe the **measles rash** – onset, appearance and spread.
cards.a:
• **Blotchy, bright red maculopapular** rash, generally **not itchy**
• Appears ~day **4–5** of illness on the **face and behind the ears** (hairline)
• Spreads **downwards** to trunk and extremities over **24–36 hours**
• Palms and soles rarely involved; lesions become **confluent**
cards.m: Measles rash runs top-down like water poured over the head.

cards.q: What happens in the **convalescent stage** of measles?
cards.a:
• Rash fades in the order it appeared, leaving a **temporary brownish staining** (fine desquamation)
• **Cough may persist 1–3 weeks**
• Temporary immune suppression → watch for secondary infection

cards.q: Which **investigations** confirm measles?
cards.a:
• Suspected clinically: 3 Cs + **Koplik spots**
• **RT-PCR** – **nasopharyngeal/throat swab** (preferred), urine or blood
• **Serology:** **measles-specific IgM** in serum within the first few days of rash

cards.q: What are the **public health actions** when you suspect measles in a KK?
cards.a:
• **Notify** the District Health Office **within 24 hours** of clinical diagnosis – do not wait for lab results
• **Isolate** the patient (airborne precautions; separate waiting area)
• Supports Malaysia’s **Measles Elimination Programme** – contact tracing and outbreak vaccination
cards.m: Measles is a 24-hour disease – suspicion is enough.

cards.q: Outline the **management** of uncomplicated measles.
cards.a:
• **No specific antiviral** – supportive care
• Plenty of fluids; treat **dehydration** from diarrhoea/vomiting
• **Antibiotics** only for secondary pneumonia, ear or eye infection
• **Vitamin A** to restore low levels and reduce complications

cards.q: What is the WHO **vitamin A dose** for a child with measles?
cards.a:
Two doses, **24 hours apart**:
• **<6 months: 50 000 IU**
• **6–11 months: 100 000 IU**
• **≥12 months: 200 000 IU**
• Third dose 2–4 weeks later if eye signs of vitamin A deficiency
cards.m: 50–100–200 by age band.

cards.q: When is **MMR** given in the Malaysian National Immunisation Programme, and why so early?
cards.a:
• **9 months** and **12 months** of age
• Early first dose because measles is common and severe in infants once maternal antibodies wane
• Live vaccine – not in pregnancy or severe immunosuppression

cards.q: List the **complications** of measles.
cards.a:
• **Otitis media**
• **Bronchopneumonia** – commonest cause of measles death
• **Diarrhoea** and dehydration
• **Encephalitis**
• Keratitis/blindness (with vitamin A deficiency); late **SSPE**

cards.q: What is **SSPE**?
cards.a:
• **Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis** – rare, **fatal** degenerative CNS disease from persistent measles virus
• Appears **7–10 years** after measles, higher risk if infected **<2 years** old
• Presents with school decline, behaviour change, **myoclonic jerks**, then dementia
• Prevented by **measles vaccination**
cards.m: Measles that comes back a decade later to destroy the brain.

cards.q: What **post-exposure** options exist for measles contacts?
cards.a:
• **MMR vaccine within 72 hours** of exposure for susceptible contacts aged ≥6 months
• **Normal human immunoglobulin within 6 days** for high-risk contacts (infants <6 months, pregnant non-immune, immunocompromised)
• Exclude case from school until **4 days after rash onset**
cards.m: Vaccine by day 3, immunoglobulin by day 6.

cards.q: What is **roseola infantum** and which age group gets it?
cards.a:
• A **common, benign, self-limiting** viral illness of infancy
• Peak age **6 months – 2 years**
• Also called **exanthem subitum** or **sixth disease**

cards.q: What causes **roseola**?
cards.a:
• **Human herpesvirus 6 (HHV-6)** – main cause
• Less commonly **HHV-7**
cards.m: Sixth disease = HHV-6.

cards.q: How is roseola **transmitted**, and when is the child infectious?
cards.a:
• **Respiratory droplets and saliva**, often from **asymptomatic shedding** adults/siblings
• Most contagious during the **febrile phase**, until the rash appears and fever has resolved for 24 hours

cards.q: What is the **classic sequence** of roseola?
cards.a:
• **Sudden high fever (>40°C) for 3–5 days**, child often surprisingly well
• **Fever subsides → then the rash appears**
• May have runny nose and mild cervical lymphadenopathy
cards.m: Fever goes, roses show.

cards.q: Describe the **rash of roseola**.
cards.a:
• **Rose-pink macular/maculopapular**, **blanching**
• Painless, non-itchy, **non-vesicular**
• Mainly **trunk** and limbs, **usually spares the face**
• Fades within **1–2 days**, **no desquamation**

cards.q: Which other examination findings may be seen in roseola?
cards.a:
• **Mild cervical lymphadenopathy**
• **Nagayama spots** – red papules on soft palate/uvula
• Mild coryza; occasionally a **bulging fontanelle** during high fever
• Rash after antibiotics is often mislabelled as **drug allergy**

cards.q: How is roseola managed in primary care?
cards.a:
• **Reassure parents** – benign and self-limiting
• **Paracetamol** for comfort/fever
• **Adequate fluid intake**
• No antibiotics, no antivirals

cards.q: What is the **most common complication** of roseola?
cards.a:
• **Febrile seizure** – during the high-fever phase (before the rash)
• HHV-6 is an important cause of febrile seizures in infants
• Usually simple and benign
cards.m: Roseola = fever, fit, then flowers.

cards.q: Which **rare serious complications** of roseola occur, and in whom?
cards.a:
• **Encephalitis**
• **Pneumonitis**
• Mainly in **immunocompromised** patients (e.g. after transplant – HHV-6 reactivation)

cards.q: When should a child with roseola be **admitted/referred**?
cards.a:
• **Complex febrile seizure** (focal, >15 min, or recurrent within 24 h)
• **Status epilepticus**
• **Prolonged lethargy**
• Signs of **secondary bacterial infection**

cards.q: How is roseola **prevented**, and is it notifiable?
cards.a:
• **Hand hygiene**; keep child at home while febrile
• **No vaccine**
• Most children are **immune by school age**
• **Not a notifiable disease**

cards.q: **Roseola vs measles** – key clinical differences?
cards.a:
• **Roseola:** rash appears **as fever settles**; child well; starts on **trunk**, spares face; fades in 1–2 days
• **Measles:** rash at **peak of fever**; child ill with **3 Cs + Koplik spots**; starts on **face/behind ears**, spreads down; leaves staining
• Roseola is not notifiable; measles is (24 h)
cards.m: Roseola: fever then rash. Measles: fever with rash.

cards.q: What is **HFMD** and who is mainly affected?
cards.a:
• A common, **contagious viral illness**
• Mainly **infants and children <5 years**
• **Endemic in Malaysia**, with periodic outbreaks in nurseries/kindergartens

cards.q: Which viruses cause HFMD, and which is most dangerous?
cards.a:
• **Enteroviruses**: **coxsackievirus A16** (commonest, usually mild), other coxsackie A/B, echoviruses
• **Enterovirus 71 (EV71)** – causes **severe neurological and cardiopulmonary** disease and deaths (Malaysian outbreaks)
• Note: slide lists **polioviruses** – they are enteroviruses but **do not cause HFMD**
cards.m: A16 = annoying; 71 = deadly.

cards.q: What are the **incubation period** and timing of blisters in HFMD?
cards.a:
• Incubation **3–6 days**
• Blisters appear **1–2 days after the fever** starts

cards.q: How long is a child with HFMD **infectious**?
cards.a:
• Until blisters have **ruptured and healed** – usually **7–10 days**
• Virus is shed in **stool for several weeks** after recovery – hygiene matters even after return

cards.q: How is HFMD **transmitted**?
cards.a:
• **Respiratory:** cough, sneeze, saliva
• **Contact:** contaminated surfaces/toys, **vesicle fluid**
• **Faecal–oral:** contact with faeces (nappy changing)

cards.q: Describe the **typical presentation** of HFMD.
cards.a:
• **Fever**, sore throat, poor appetite, fatigue, headache
• **Painful oral ulcers** – tongue, buccal mucosa, palate
• **Flat/oval vesicles or maculopapular rash** on **palms and soles**, also **buttocks and genital area**
• Rash is usually **not itchy**

cards.q: What is the MOH **clinical case definition** of HFMD, and how is a case confirmed?
cards.a:
• Any child (MOH: ≤10 years) with **mouth/tongue ulcer** AND **maculopapular rash and/or vesicles on palms and soles**, **with or without fever** = **suspected case**
• **Confirmed:** lab detection of enterovirus **or** epidemiological link to a lab-confirmed case
• Note: slide labels the clinical definition 'confirmed'; it defines a **suspected** case

cards.q: What are the **notification rules** for HFMD in Malaysia?
cards.a:
• Notify the District Health Office **within 24 hours** of a **suspected** case
• **Laboratory confirmation is NOT required** for notification
• Triggers **outbreak management** at the nursery/kindergarten
cards.m: HFMD: suspect it, report it – today.

cards.q: How is **uncomplicated HFMD** managed at a KK?
cards.a:
• **Reassurance and explanation** – usually mild and self-limiting (7–10 days)
• **Symptomatic:** paracetamol; cold soft foods/drinks for mouth pain
• **Maintain hydration**
• Careful hygiene; **notify**
• Teach parents the **danger signs**

cards.q: Which **general (non-neurological) criteria** warrant admission in HFMD?
cards.a:
• **Unable to tolerate oral feeds** / risk of dehydration
• **Toxic-looking** / clinically very ill
• Serious alternative diagnosis cannot be excluded
• **Hyperpyrexia persisting >48 hours**
• **Parents unable to cope** / inadequate social support

cards.q: Which **neurological danger signs** in HFMD need urgent referral?
cards.a:
• **Increased lethargy/drowsiness**
• **Myoclonic jerks** (startles, especially in sleep)
• **Altered sensorium**
• **Seizures**
• Also: persistent vomiting, ataxia, limb weakness
cards.m: A sleepy, jerky, vomiting child with HFMD = EV71 brainstem trouble.

cards.q: Which signs suggest **cardiac/cardiopulmonary involvement** in HFMD?
cards.a:
• **Tachycardia** out of proportion to fever, **breathlessness**
• **Hypotension**, **low pulse volume**, poor perfusion
• **Arrhythmia**
• **Murmur or gallop rhythm**
• → Immediate hospital referral

cards.q: Why can **EV71** HFMD kill a previously well child within hours?
cards.a:
• EV71 causes **brainstem encephalitis**
• → sympathetic surge → **neurogenic pulmonary oedema** and **cardiopulmonary failure**
• Deterioration can be rapid, often within 2–5 days of onset – hence strict danger-sign advice

cards.q: What **prevention advice** do you give families and nurseries about HFMD?
cards.a:
• **Frequent hand washing** with soap and water
• Cover coughs/sneezes; avoid close contact with sick children
• **Clean and disinfect** toys, utensils, toilet floors
• Do not share personal items; wash them with detergent
• **Do not rupture blisters**

cards.q: When can a child with HFMD return to **nursery/kindergarten**?
cards.a:
• Keep at home until **fever has settled and all blisters have dried/healed** (usually 7–10 days)
• During clusters the health office may **order temporary closure** of the premises
• Continue strict hand hygiene – stool shedding continues for weeks

cards.q: **HFMD vs herpangina vs varicella** – how do you tell them apart?
cards.a:
• **HFMD:** oral ulcers (anterior mouth) + vesicles on **palms, soles, buttocks**; not itchy
• **Herpangina:** vesicles/ulcers on **posterior pharynx/soft palate only**, no hand–foot rash
• **Varicella:** **itchy**, **centripetal** (trunk) vesicles in crops, different stages
cards.m: Hands and feet = HFMD; throat only = herpangina; trunk itch = pox.

cards.q: What causes **dengue**, and why is a second infection more dangerous?
cards.a:
• **Dengue virus** (flavivirus), **4 serotypes: DEN-1 to DEN-4**
• Vectors: **Aedes aegypti** and **Aedes albopictus** (day-biting mosquitoes)
• Infection gives lifelong immunity only to **that serotype**
• **Subsequent infection with another serotype** → higher risk of severe dengue (antibody-dependent enhancement)
cards.m: Second dengue, different serotype = double danger.

cards.q: What are the **three phases** of dengue illness?
cards.a:
• **Febrile phase:** high fever, usually **2–7 days**
• **Critical phase:** around **defervescence (≈day 3–7)**, lasts **24–48 h** – **plasma leakage**, shock, bleeding
• **Recovery phase:** **48–72 h** – reabsorption of leaked fluid; risk of **fluid overload**
cards.m: Fever → Fall (leak) → Fill-up (reabsorb).

cards.q: Why is the moment the **fever settles** in dengue so dangerous?
cards.a:
• Defervescence coincides with the **critical phase** of **plasma leakage**
• Patient may **feel better** while haematocrit rises and shock develops
• So patients need **daily review** through days 3–7 even when afebrile
cards.m: In dengue, 'fever gone' does not mean 'danger gone'.

cards.q: List the **warning signs** of dengue (MOH CPG).
cards.a:
• **Abdominal pain or tenderness**
• **Persistent vomiting**
• **Clinical fluid accumulation** (pleural effusion, ascites)
• **Mucosal bleeding**
• **Lethargy/restlessness**
• **Liver enlargement >2 cm**
• Lab: **rising HCT with rapid fall in platelets**
cards.m: A-V-F-M-L-L-HCT: Abdomen, Vomiting, Fluid, Mucosa, Lethargy, Liver, Labs.

cards.q: What key points do you cover in the **history** of suspected dengue?
cards.a:
• Onset, duration and pattern of fever
• **Warning signs**; change in mental state
• **Oral fluid intake and urine output**
• **Exposure:** family/neighbours ill, hotspot area, travel; **jungle trekking/waterfall** (consider leptospirosis, typhus, malaria)
• Comorbidities, pregnancy

cards.q: What should the **physical examination** in dengue focus on?
cards.a:
• **Mental state and GCS**
• **Hydration**
• Vital signs and perfusion – **CCTVR**: colour, capillary refill, temperature of extremities, pulse volume, rate
• **Tachypnoea/acidotic breathing/pleural effusion**
• **Abdominal tenderness, hepatomegaly, ascites**
• **Bleeding** manifestations

cards.q: What is the 'isles of white in a sea of red' rash in dengue?
cards.a:
• **Convalescent (recovery-phase) rash** – confluent erythema/petechiae with small islands of normal skin
• Often **itchy**; appears as patient improves
• A sign of recovery, not of bleeding risk
cards.m: White islands in a red sea = recovering dengue.

cards.q: How is the **tourniquet test** done and interpreted?
cards.a:
• Inflate BP cuff **midway between systolic and diastolic** for **5 minutes**
• Count petechiae in a **2.5 cm × 2.5 cm** square on the forearm
• **≥10 petechiae = positive** – capillary fragility, supports dengue
• A negative test does not exclude dengue

cards.q: What is the **notification** requirement for dengue?
cards.a:
• Notify a **suspected** dengue case **within 24 hours** to the nearest District Health Office
• Register in **e-dengue**
• Enables vector control (fogging, source reduction) around the patient’s home

cards.q: When are **NS1 antigen** and **dengue IgM** most useful?
cards.a:
• **NS1 antigen:** early febrile phase, **day 1–5**
• **IgM:** from about **day 5** onwards (slide: primary infection IgM day 6–10)
• **Secondary infection:** **IgG** rises early and markedly (slide: >day 7), IgM may be low
• Negative NS1 after day 5 does **not** exclude dengue
cards.m: NS1 = Number 1 test (first 5 days); IgM = later.

cards.q: What does the **rapid combo test (RCT)** detect?
cards.a:
• **NS1 antigen + IgM + IgG** on one strip
• Covers both early (NS1) and later (antibody) phases – widely used in KKs
• Positive result supports a **suspected** dengue case for notification

cards.q: What is the role of **RT-PCR** in dengue?
cards.a:
• Useful in the **early febrile phase (≤5 days)**
• **Identifies the serotype**
• Very accurate but **expensive** and **not routinely used** in primary care

cards.q: What **FBC changes** are typical in dengue?
cards.a:
• **Leucopenia** in the early febrile phase
• **Thrombocytopenia** – falling platelets
• **Rising haematocrit** → **plasma leakage** (haemoconcentration)
• Always interpret HCT against the patient’s **baseline**

cards.q: Which **combined FBC trend** signals plasma leakage and need for admission?
cards.a:
• **Rising HCT** at the same time as a **rapid drop in platelet count**
• Indicates entry into the **critical phase** → admit
• Platelet count alone does not predict leakage
cards.m: HCT up + platelets down = leaking.

cards.q: Besides FBC, which **monitoring tests** are done in hospitalised dengue?
cards.a:
• **LFT** (transaminitis, liver involvement)
• **Renal profile and electrolytes**
• **Coagulation profile**
• **ABG** (acidosis in shock)
• Also blood glucose, serum lactate in severe cases

cards.q: Which dengue patients can be **managed as outpatients**?
cards.a:
• **Tolerating oral intake**, adequate urine output
• **Stable vital signs**, **no warning signs**
• **Stable serial HCT**
• **No bleeding**, no change in mental state
• **No comorbidity, not pregnant**
• Must have **daily follow-up from day 3** of illness

cards.q: Why must outpatient dengue patients be reviewed **daily from day 3**?
cards.a:
• Critical phase (leakage) usually begins around **day 3–7**, near defervescence
• Daily **clinical review + FBC/HCT** detects warning signs early
• Continue until clearly through the critical phase

cards.q: What are the **hospital admission criteria** for dengue?
cards.a:
• **Any warning sign**
• **Unable to tolerate oral fluids** or **reduced urine output**
• **Bleeding** or **organ impairment**
• **Special groups:** elderly, **pregnant**, comorbidities (e.g. diabetes, heart/renal disease)
• **Rising HCT with dropping platelets**

cards.q: Which drugs and procedures must be **avoided** in dengue?
cards.a:
• **NSAIDs** (ibuprofen, diclofenac, mefenamic acid) and **aspirin** – platelet dysfunction, bleeding, gastritis
• **Intramuscular injections** – haematoma
• Steroids (no benefit)
• Use **paracetamol** only (adult max 4 g/day)
cards.m: Dengue: Paracetamol, Pee, Plenty of fluids – no NSAIDs, no needles in muscle.

cards.q: What does the **dengue home care card** advise?
cards.a:
• **Adequate rest**; **plenty of oral fluids** (water, juices, ORS – not just plain water)
• **Paracetamol** and tepid sponging for fever; no NSAIDs/aspirin
• **Monitor urine output**
• **Return immediately** if warning signs: abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, bleeding, drowsiness/restlessness, no urine for 4–6 h, cold clammy limbs
• Attend daily review

cards.q: How does **inpatient monitoring** differ across the three dengue phases?
cards.a:
• **Febrile:** watch for progression – **daily FBC**, clinical signs, hydration
• **Critical:** monitor **every 2–4 h** (**every 15–30 min in shock**); **HCT before and after fluid boluses**; watch for leakage, shock, bleeding
• **Recovery:** watch for **fluid overload**; **taper or stop IV fluids**

cards.q: What **maintenance fluid rate** do the slides give for adult dengue, and which weight is used in obesity?
cards.a:
• **Non-obese:** **1.2–1.5 ml/kg/h**
• **Obese (BMI >27.5 kg/m²):** calculate using **adjusted body weight (ABW)**, not actual weight
• Prevents fluid overload in obese patients

cards.q: How are **ideal and adjusted body weight** calculated for dengue fluid therapy?
cards.a:
• **IBW female = 45.5 kg + 0.91 × (height cm − 152)**
• **IBW male = 50.0 kg + 0.91 × (height cm − 152)**
• **ABW = IBW + 0.4 × (actual weight − IBW)**
cards.m: ABW = ideal plus 40% of the excess.

cards.q: What are the signs of the **recovery phase** in dengue, and its main risk?
cards.a:
• Return of **appetite** and well-being, **diuresis**
• HCT **stabilises or falls**, platelets and WBC start rising
• **Bradycardia** and convalescent itchy rash
• Main risk: **fluid overload** (pulmonary oedema) if IV fluids are not reduced

cards.q: What is the **notification** requirement for typhus in Malaysia?
cards.a:
• Notify the District Health Office **within 7 days** from the date of diagnosis
• Contrast: dengue, measles and HFMD are **24-hour** notifications

cards.q: How is **typhus** spread, and what are the risk factors?
cards.a:
• Rickettsial infections spread by **fleas, lice and chiggers (mite larvae)**
• Risks: **poor sanitation**, **crowded living**, exposure to infected fleas/lice, travel to outbreak areas, outdoor/jungle exposure

cards.q: What causes **scrub typhus**, how is it transmitted, and where?
cards.a:
• **Orientia tsutsugamushi**
• **Mite-borne** – bite of infected **chiggers** (larval trombiculid mites)
• **Rural Southeast Asia**, Indian subcontinent, northern Australia ('tsutsugamushi triangle') – includes Malaysia
cards.m: Scrub = scrubland chiggers.

cards.q: What causes **murine typhus**, and how is it spread?
cards.a:
• **Rickettsia typhi**
• **Flea-borne** – infected **rat and cat fleas** (flea faeces into bite wounds)
• Tropical, subtropical and temperate regions worldwide; often **urban/port** areas
cards.m: Murine = mouse/rat fleas.

cards.q: What causes **epidemic typhus**, and in what setting?
cards.a:
• **Rickettsia prowazekii**
• **Louse-borne** – infected **body lice**
• Settings of **extreme overcrowding** – refugee camps, war, prisons, homelessness

cards.q: What is an **eschar**, and why must you search for it?
cards.a:
• A **painless black necrotic crust** with red rim at the **chigger bite site**
• Strongly suggests **scrub typhus**
• Often hidden: **groin, axilla, waistband, under breasts, scrotum** – examine the whole body
• Usually with **regional lymphadenopathy**
cards.m: Look for a cigarette-burn-like scab where clothes are tight.

cards.q: Describe the **clinical features of scrub typhus**.
cards.a:
• Onset **within ~10 days** of the bite
• **Fever and chills, headache, myalgia**
• **Eschar** + **enlarged lymph nodes**
• **Maculopapular rash on the trunk** spreading to extremities
• Dry cough; severe cases: pneumonitis, meningoencephalitis

cards.q: Which **exposure history** should make you think of scrub typhus in Malaysia?
cards.a:
• **Oil palm/rubber plantation** and agricultural workers, farmers
• **Jungle trekking, camping**, soldiers, Orang Asli communities
• Clearing grass/scrub, **waterfall** outings
• Fever + eschar in such a patient → treat empirically

cards.q: What are the **laboratory criteria** for diagnosing scrub typhus (MOH case definition)?
cards.a:
• **Indirect immunoperoxidase test:** **IgG titre ≥1:400** or **IgM titre ≥1:50**
• Or **four-fold rise** in antibody titre in paired sera
• Or isolation of the organism (historically 'Rickettsia tsutsugamushi') by inoculating patient blood into mice
cards.m: IgM 50, IgG 400.

cards.q: What is the **Weil-Felix test** and its limitation?
cards.a:
• Cheap **heterophile agglutination** test using **Proteus antigens**
• **OX-K** positive → scrub typhus; **OX-19** → murine/epidemic typhus
• **Poor sensitivity and specificity** – supportive only; immunoperoxidase/IFA preferred

cards.q: What is the **first-line treatment** of typhus, with doses?
cards.a:
• **Doxycycline**, usually for **7–10 days**
• **Adults: 100 mg twice daily**
• **Children <45 kg: 2.2 mg/kg twice daily**
• Fever usually settles within **24–48 h** – lack of response questions the diagnosis
cards.m: Doxy for the bugs that bite: ticks, mites, fleas, lice.

cards.q: Can **doxycycline** be used in children under 8 for rickettsial infection?
cards.a:
• **Yes** – it is the **drug of choice at any age** for suspected rickettsial disease
• Short courses carry minimal risk of dental staining (unlike older tetracyclines)
• Delay in treatment causes more harm than the drug

cards.q: What are the **alternatives to doxycycline** for scrub typhus?
cards.a:
• **Azithromycin** – preferred in **pregnancy** and an option in young children
• **Chloramphenicol** – older alternative
• Rifampicin in areas with poor doxycycline response

cards.q: What is the **referral rule** for typhus, and which complications are feared?
cards.a:
• Slides: **all typhus cases should be referred to hospital**
• Complications: **pneumonitis/ARDS**, **myocarditis**, **meningoencephalitis**, acute kidney injury, multi-organ failure
• Start doxycycline early – do not wait for serology

cards.q: What causes **typhoid (enteric) fever**?
cards.a:
• **Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi** (typhoid) or **Paratyphi** A/B/C (paratyphoid)
• Multisystemic, potentially life-threatening
• Paratyphoid is generally **milder**; diagnosis and treatment are similar
• **Humans are the only reservoir**

cards.q: How is typhoid transmitted, and who is the commonest source?
cards.a:
• **Faecal–oral** – ingestion of **contaminated food or water**
• **Food handlers** are the most common carriers
• Common where hygiene, safe water and sanitation are poor
cards.m: Typhoid travels by the 4 Fs: food, fingers, faeces, flies.

cards.q: What are the **notification** rules for typhoid/paratyphoid in Malaysia?
cards.a:
• **Suspected, probable and confirmed** cases must be notified **within 7 days** of diagnosis
• Only **laboratory-confirmed** cases are registered
• Triggers source tracing (food premises, food handlers, water)

cards.q: Describe the **clinical features** of typhoid fever.
cards.a:
• **Prolonged fever** – classically **step-ladder** rise in week 1 – with malaise, headache
• Anorexia, **weight loss**
• Abdominal pain, **constipation** (more often than diarrhoea in adults), vomiting
• Abdominal tenderness, **splenomegaly**, **relative bradycardia**
• **Rose spots**; bloody stools in complicated cases
cards.m: Typhoid climbs the stairs: fever steps up day by day.

cards.q: What are **rose spots**?
cards.a:
• Faint **salmon-pink, blanching macules** 2–4 mm
• On the **abdomen, chest and back**, in small crops
• Usually in the **second week**; hard to see on darker skin
• Contain bacteria – a classic but often absent sign

cards.q: What is **relative bradycardia** and in which fevers is it seen?
cards.a:
• Pulse **lower than expected** for the degree of fever (pulse–temperature dissociation, **Faget sign**)
• Classic in **typhoid**
• Also in typhus, legionella, leptospirosis, dengue, yellow fever, drug fever
cards.m: Hot patient, slow heart – think typhoid.

cards.q: How are typhoid cases **classified**?
cards.a:
• **Suspected:** fulfils clinical criteria
• **Probable:** suspected + **positive serology** (or antigen test)
• **Confirmed:** clinical criteria + **laboratory isolation**
• **Relapse:** recurrence with positive culture **<3 months**
• **Reinfection:** recurrence with positive culture **>3 months**
cards.m: Relapse is early (<3 m), reinfection is later (>3 m).

cards.q: What **history** is essential in suspected typhoid?
cards.a:
• Onset and symptoms; **treatment already taken** (antibiotics reduce culture yield)
• **Travel** in the **7–21 days** before illness
• **Food and drink history**, including food premises
• Contact with typhoid/paratyphoid cases
• **Vaccination status**; list of **close contacts**

cards.q: Which **specific tests** diagnose typhoid, and when is each best?
cards.a:
• **Blood culture** – best in the **first week** (before antibiotics)
• **Stool culture** – more often positive from week 2–3; screens carriers
• **Bone marrow culture** – **most sensitive**, stays positive despite antibiotics
• **PCR** – detects S. Typhi in **asymptomatic carriers/food handlers**; more sensitive than stool culture
• Plus FBC, RFT, LFT
cards.m: BASU: Blood (wk 1), Antibodies, Stool (wk 2–3), Urine – blood first.

cards.q: Why is the **Widal test** unreliable for diagnosing typhoid?
cards.a:
• Measures **agglutinating antibodies** (O and H) – rises late (week 2+)
• **False positives**: past infection, vaccination, cross-reacting infections, high background titres in endemic areas
• **False negatives**: early disease, prior antibiotics
• A single titre is **not diagnostic** – culture is the standard

cards.q: Which patients with typhoid must be **referred immediately**?
cards.a:
• **Moderate to severe illness**, or confirmed typhoid with **complications**
• **Hypotension or shock**; **severe dehydration**
• **Persistent vomiting**/unable to tolerate oral intake
• **Pregnant women, infants, elderly, immunocompromised** with suspected typhoid
• Slides: adults with typhoid are referred to hospital

cards.q: Which **antibiotics** are used for typhoid in Malaysia?
cards.a:
• **Severe/inpatient:** **IV ceftriaxone**
• **Uncomplicated:** **oral azithromycin** (e.g. 7 days)
• **Fluoroquinolone (ciprofloxacin) resistance is common** in Asian isolates – avoid empirically
• Guided by culture sensitivity; complete the full course

cards.q: What are the classic **complications** of typhoid and when do they occur?
cards.a:
• Usually in the **third week**
• **Intestinal perforation** and **GI haemorrhage** (ulcerated **Peyer patches** of the terminal ileum)
• Typhoid encephalopathy, hepatitis, myocarditis, cholecystitis
• Relapse; chronic carriage
cards.m: Week 1 fever, week 2 spots, week 3 holes.

cards.q: What is a **chronic typhoid carrier**, and how are food handlers managed?
cards.a:
• Excretes S. Typhi **>1 year** after infection – usually from the **gallbladder** (gallstones increase risk)
• Infected/carrier **food handlers must not handle food** until cleared
• MOH: discharge after **3 consecutive negative stool cultures**; follow-up stool cultures at **1, 2, 3, 6 and 12 months**

cards.q: Compare the two **typhoid vaccines**.
cards.a:
• **Oral live attenuated Ty21a:** liquid or enteric-coated capsules, **3 doses 2 days apart** (not in pregnancy/immunosuppression)
• **Injectable Vi capsular polysaccharide (Vi CPS):** **single IM dose**
• **Food handlers:** regular **booster every 3 years**
cards.m: Ty21a = Taken by mouth ×3; Vi = Very simple, one jab.

cards.q: What **hygiene advice** prevents typhoid?
cards.a:
• **Hand washing with soap** before eating/handling food and after the toilet (or sanitiser)
• Drink only **boiled or bottled water**
• Avoid **uncooked vegetables and raw food**
• Cook seafood, fish and meat **thoroughly**
• Avoid ready-to-eat food from **roadside vendors**
cards.m: Boil it, cook it, peel it – or forget it.

cards.q: What causes **scarlet fever** and the rash?
cards.a:
• **Group A Streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes)**, usually pharyngitis
• Strains producing **pyrogenic (erythrogenic) exotoxin**
• Toxin causes an inflammatory response and **dilatation of dermal vessels** → rash

cards.q: Who gets scarlet fever, how does it spread, and what is the incubation period?
cards.a:
• Most common in children **5–15 years**
• Crowded settings – schools, nursing homes
• Spread by **respiratory droplets, direct contact, fomites**
• Incubation **~2–5 days**

cards.q: Describe the **rash** of scarlet fever.
cards.a:
• Diffuse fine red rash that **feels rough like sandpaper**
• Starts on neck/chest, spreads to trunk and limbs
• **Blanches**; most intense in skin folds
• **Peels** as it fades
cards.m: Scarlet = sandpaper.

cards.q: What are **Pastia lines**?
cards.a:
• **Brighter red linear** accentuation of the rash in **skin creases** – **axilla, elbow (antecubital fossa), groin**
• Due to capillary fragility in folds
• Do not blanch completely

cards.q: What facial sign is typical of scarlet fever?
cards.a:
• **Flushed cheeks** with **circumoral pallor** – a pale area around the mouth
• Contrast: Kawasaki has **red, cracked lips**
cards.m: Red face, white moustache.

cards.q: How does the **tongue** change in scarlet fever?
cards.a:
• **Early:** **white strawberry tongue** – white coating with red swollen papillae
• **Later (day 4–5):** **red strawberry tongue** – coating peels off
• Strawberry tongue also occurs in **Kawasaki disease** and TSS

cards.q: What **throat and neck** findings accompany scarlet fever?
cards.a:
• **Very red throat**, red **swollen tonsils** with **white patches/streaks of pus**
• **Palatal petechiae**
• Tender, swollen **anterior cervical lymph nodes**
• Plus fever ≥38°C, sore throat, painful swallowing, headache, vomiting, abdominal pain

cards.q: Which **investigations** support scarlet fever?
cards.a:
• **Throat (or nasal) swab culture**
• **Rapid streptococcal antigen test**
• **ASO titre** – evidence of recent strep (useful for complications)
• Blood/urine – high WBC; albuminuria, haematuria (nephritis), haemolytic anaemia

cards.q: What is the **antibiotic treatment** of scarlet fever?
cards.a:
• **Phenoxymethylpenicillin (penicillin V)** or **amoxicillin** for **10 days**
• **Penicillin allergy:** **erythromycin** (or other macrolide)
• Severe pharyngitis: may need IV fluids and IV antibiotics
• Antihistamine for itch
cards.m: Strep throat: 10 days of penicillin – no shortcuts.

cards.q: Why must the **full 10-day course** be completed in streptococcal pharyngitis/scarlet fever?
cards.a:
• To **eradicate GAS from the pharynx**
• This **prevents acute rheumatic fever** (if started within 9 days of onset)
• Antibiotics do **not** reliably prevent **post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis**

cards.q: When can a child with scarlet fever return to **school**?
cards.a:
• After **24 hours of antibiotics** **and** clinically improving
• Reinforce **hand and environmental hygiene**
cards.m: 24 hours on penicillin, then back to class.

cards.q: List the **suppurative complications** of GAS infection/scarlet fever.
cards.a:
• **Peritonsillar (quinsy)** or retropharyngeal abscess
• **Otitis media**, **sinusitis**
• **Necrotising fasciitis**
• Streptococcal **bacteraemia**
• **Meningitis**, brain abscess

cards.q: List the **non-suppurative complications** of GAS infection and their timing.
cards.a:
• **Acute rheumatic fever** – ~**2–4 weeks** after pharyngitis
• **Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis** – ~**1–3 weeks** after throat (3–6 weeks after skin) infection
• **Post-streptococcal reactive arthritis**
• **Streptococcal toxic shock syndrome**
cards.m: Kidney comes first (1–3 wk), heart a bit later (2–4 wk).

cards.q: **Scarlet fever vs Kawasaki disease** – how do you tell them apart?
cards.a:
• Both: fever, rash, strawberry tongue, later peeling
• **Scarlet fever:** age 5–15, **exudative tonsillitis**, sandpaper rash, **circumoral pallor**, **no conjunctivitis**; settles within 24–48 h of penicillin
• **Kawasaki:** usually <5 years, **bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis**, **red cracked lips**, swollen hands/feet, fever ≥5 days **despite antibiotics**
cards.m: Pus on tonsils and better on penicillin = scarlet; red eyes and no response = Kawasaki.

cards.q: What is **toxic shock syndrome (TSS)** and which organisms cause it?
cards.a:
• A **severe, acute, toxin-mediated** illness
• **Staphylococcus aureus** (most common – **TSST-1** and enterotoxins)
• **Group A Streptococcus** (streptococcal TSS)

cards.q: Why does TSS cause **shock so rapidly** (pathophysiology)?
cards.a:
• Toxins act as **superantigens**
• Bind **MHC class II** and **T-cell receptors** non-specifically → activate up to 20% of T cells
• **Massive cytokine release** → capillary leak, vasodilatation, **shock and multi-organ failure**
cards.m: Superantigen = switches on the whole immune army at once.

cards.q: What are the key **risk factors** for TSS?
cards.a:
• **Tampon use** (menstrual TSS)
• **Nasal packing**
• **Recent wound/surgical infection**, burns
• Postpartum infection, skin infection after varicella (streptococcal TSS)

cards.q: Describe the **clinical presentation** of TSS.
cards.a:
• **Sudden high fever**
• **Vomiting and diarrhoea**
• **Sunburn-like diffuse rash** (macular erythroderma)
• **Hypotension/shock**, confusion
• Later **desquamation**
cards.m: Tampon + sunburn + shock = TSS.

cards.q: When and where does **desquamation** occur in TSS?
cards.a:
• Usually **1–2 weeks after onset**
• Especially **palms and soles** (fingertips)
• A late, retrospective clue to the diagnosis

cards.q: What are the **CDC clinical criteria** for staphylococcal TSS?
cards.a:
• **Fever ≥38.9°C**
• **Diffuse macular erythroderma**
• **Desquamation 1–2 weeks** after onset
• **Hypotension** (adult SBP ≤90 mmHg)
• **≥3 organ systems:** GI, muscular (CK), mucous membranes, renal, hepatic, haematological (platelets <100), CNS
cards.m: Fever, Flush, Flaking, Falling BP, Failure of 3 organs.

cards.q: What is the **primary-care management** of suspected TSS?
cards.a:
• **Stabilise ABC** – oxygen, **IV fluids**
• **Remove the source** – tampon, nasal or wound packing
• **Empirical antibiotics:** **ceftriaxone + clindamycin**
• **Urgent hospital transfer**

cards.q: Why is **clindamycin** added in toxic shock syndrome?
cards.a:
• It **inhibits bacterial protein synthesis** → **switches off toxin production**
• Effective even with high bacterial load in stationary phase (Eagle effect limits beta-lactams)
• Always combined with a bactericidal agent
cards.m: Clindamycin cuts the toxin factory’s power.

cards.q: How does **streptococcal TSS** differ from staphylococcal TSS?
cards.a:
• Usually follows **soft-tissue infection** (e.g. necrotising fasciitis, infected varicella), with **severe pain**
• **Blood cultures usually positive** (rare in staph TSS)
• Rash less common; **mortality higher** (30–70%)
• May need urgent surgical debridement

cards.q: How is TSS **prevented**?
cards.a:
• Good **hygiene** and **wound care**
• **Tampons:** lowest absorbency needed, **change every 4–8 h**, alternate with pads, avoid overnight use
• Prior TSS → avoid tampons (recurrence risk)

cards.q: What organism causes **meningococcaemia** and how does it spread?
cards.a:
• **Neisseria meningitidis** – **Gram-negative diplococcus**; serogroups A, B, C, W, Y
• Colonises the **nasopharynx** of healthy carriers (teenagers, young adults)
• Spread by **respiratory droplets/close contact** (kissing, shared dormitories, Hajj)

cards.q: Describe the classic **rash** of meningococcaemia.
cards.a:
• **Non-blanching petechial or purpuric** rash, often on limbs/trunk
• May **start as a blanching maculopapular** rash – do not be falsely reassured
• Can progress rapidly to **purpura fulminans** (large necrotic areas)
• Fever + non-blanching rash = **treat immediately**
cards.m: Spots that won’t fade = time to act.

cards.q: How is the **glass (tumbler) test** performed and interpreted?
cards.a:
• Press the side of a **clear glass** firmly against the rash
• Rash **fades** = blanching (erythema)
• Rash **still visible through the glass** = **non-blanching** (petechiae/purpura)
• Non-blanching rash + fever → suspect **meningococcal septicaemia**; harder to see on dark skin – check conjunctivae, palms, soles

cards.q: What are the **early warning features** of meningococcal sepsis that appear before the classic rash?
cards.a:
• **Leg pain** / refusing to walk
• **Cold hands and feet**, prolonged capillary refill
• **Abnormal skin colour** – pallor, mottling
• Tachycardia, tachypnoea, drowsiness
• Classic meningism (neck stiffness, photophobia) may be **absent** in septicaemia
cards.m: Cold, colour, cramps (leg pain) – before the spots.

cards.q: How is meningococcal disease **diagnosed**?
cards.a:
• Primarily a **clinical diagnosis** – treat on suspicion
• **Culture and sensitivity** – blood, CSF (Gram-negative diplococci)
• **Antigen/DNA detection by PCR** (blood, CSF) – stays positive after antibiotics

cards.q: What **pre-hospital benzylpenicillin** dose is recommended for suspected meningococcaemia?
cards.a:
• Treatment is **extremely urgent** – give **before reaching hospital**
• **Adult: benzylpenicillin 2.4 g IV or IM**
• **Child: 60 mg/kg IV/IM (max 2.4 g)**
• IM into thigh/deltoid is acceptable if no IV access
cards.m: Don’t drive, inject first.

cards.q: What is the **ceftriaxone** alternative for suspected meningococcaemia?
cards.a:
• **Ceftriaxone 2 g IV or IM** (adults)
• **Child >1 month: 50 mg/kg (max 2 g)**
• Preferred in **penicillin allergy** (non-anaphylactic) and covers other meningitis organisms

cards.q: Why must antibiotics **not be delayed** for investigations in suspected meningococcaemia?
cards.a:
• Can progress from first symptoms to **death within hours**
• **Early antibiotics** reduce mortality and limb loss
• Take blood culture only if it causes **no delay**; **PCR** still detects the organism after antibiotics
• **Never** do a lumbar puncture in primary care before transfer

cards.q: Who needs **chemoprophylaxis** after a meningococcal case, and with what?
cards.a:
• **Close contacts** in the 7 days before onset – household, dormitory, kissing contacts
• **Rifampicin** 600 mg twice daily for 2 days (child 10 mg/kg; <1 month 5 mg/kg)
• **Ciprofloxacin** 500 mg single oral dose
• **Ceftriaxone** 250 mg IM single dose (child 125 mg) – preferred in **pregnancy**
• Give ASAP (ideally within 24 h)
cards.m: R-C-C: Rifampicin, Cipro, Ceftriaxone.

cards.q: Which **meningococcal vaccines** exist and which is required for pilgrims?
cards.a:
• **MenACWY** (quadrivalent conjugate) – **mandatory for Hajj/Umrah** pilgrims (Saudi requirement)
• **MenB** – separate vaccine for serogroup B
• The two are **not interchangeable** – target different serogroups

cards.q: List the **complications** of meningococcal septicaemia.
cards.a:
• **Septic shock** and **DIC**
• **Purpura fulminans** → skin necrosis, **limb/digit amputation**
• **Waterhouse–Friderichsen syndrome** (adrenal haemorrhage)
• Meningitis sequelae: **sensorineural hearing loss**, seizures, cognitive impairment
• Mortality ~10% even with treatment

cards.q: What must you **counsel** when giving **rifampicin** prophylaxis?
cards.a:
• Turns **urine, tears and sweat orange-red**; stains **soft contact lenses**
• **Reduces efficacy of hormonal contraceptives** – use barrier methods
• Interacts with warfarin, anticonvulsants, antiretrovirals
• Avoid in pregnancy and severe liver disease – use ceftriaxone
cards.m: Rifampicin: red fluids, failed pill.

cards.q: What is **Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS)**?
cards.a:
• A **severe, rare hypersensitivity reaction** affecting **skin and mucous membranes**
• **Full-thickness epidermal necrosis** → **epidermal detachment**
• Usually **drug-induced**; a dermatological emergency

cards.q: How are **SJS, SJS/TEN overlap and TEN** distinguished?
cards.a:
By **body surface area (BSA) of epidermal detachment**:
• **SJS: <10%**
• **SJS/TEN overlap: 10–30%**
• **Toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN): >30%**
cards.m: 10 and 30 – the two cut-offs.

cards.q: Which **drugs** most commonly cause SJS/TEN?
cards.a:
• **Anticonvulsants:** **carbamazepine**, phenytoin, **lamotrigine**, phenobarbitone
• **Allopurinol**
• **Sulphonamides** (e.g. cotrimoxazole); beta-lactams less often
• **Nevirapine**
• **Oxicam NSAIDs** (piroxicam, meloxicam)
• Note: slide lists 'salicylates' – the classic NSAID culprits are oxicams
cards.m: CALMS: Carbamazepine, Allopurinol, Lamotrigine, Meloxicam/oxicams, Sulphonamides (+ nevirapine).

cards.q: Which **genetic test** is done before carbamazepine in Malaysia, and why?
cards.a:
• **HLA-B*15:02** genotyping – strongly associated with **carbamazepine-induced SJS/TEN** in **Han Chinese, Malays, Thais** and other Southeast Asians (also phenytoin)
• Positive → **avoid carbamazepine** (and related aromatic anticonvulsants)
• **HLA-B*58:01** → **allopurinol** SJS risk
cards.m: 1502 = carbamazepine; 5801 = allopurinol.

cards.q: Which **infections** can trigger SJS?
cards.a:
• **Mycoplasma pneumoniae** – commonest infective trigger, especially in **children** (mucositis-predominant)
• **Herpes simplex virus**

cards.q: What is the typical **latency** between starting a drug and SJS onset?
cards.a:
• Usually **4–28 days** (up to ~8 weeks) after starting a new drug
• Re-exposure can trigger a reaction within **hours to days**
• Always ask about **drugs started in the last 2 months**

cards.q: Describe the **prodrome** of SJS.
cards.a:
• **1–3 days** of **fever, sore throat, cough, malaise**
• Looks like a **flu-like illness** – may be wrongly treated with more drugs
• Then skin and mucosal lesions appear

cards.q: Describe the **acute skin lesions** of SJS.
cards.a:
• Appear ~3–4 days after prodrome
• **Painful red or purplish (dusky) macules** → **atypical target lesions**, mainly trunk/face
• **Blisters** form; skin **peels off easily**
• **Pain out of proportion** to the rash
• Contrast: erythema multiforme – typical raised targets, acral, often HSV
cards.m: Painful dusky skin + sore mouth after a new drug = SJS.

cards.q: What is the **Nikolsky sign**?
cards.a:
• Gentle **lateral pressure** on apparently normal skin → **epidermis shears off**
• **Positive** in **SJS/TEN**, staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome and pemphigus vulgaris
• Negative in bullous pemphigoid (subepidermal, tense blisters)

cards.q: Which **mucosal sites** are involved in SJS?
cards.a:
• **Oral:** painful ulcers, **haemorrhagic crusted lips**
• **Ocular:** red eyes, conjunctivitis, pseudomembranes
• **Genital:** sores/erosions
• Usually **≥2 mucosal sites** – helps distinguish from simple drug rash

cards.q: Which **investigations** are relevant in SJS, and should they delay referral?
cards.a:
• **Skin biopsy** – confirms **full-thickness epidermal necrosis**
• **FBC, LFT, renal profile, electrolytes** – systemic effects
• **Urgent ophthalmic assessment** if eyes involved
• **Do NOT delay referral** for investigations

cards.q: Outline the **management** of SJS/TEN.
cards.a:
• **Stop the suspected drug immediately** (single most important step)
• **Supportive care:** IV fluids, **pain control**, nutrition (possibly NG feeding), wound and eye care
• **Urgent referral** to **ICU or burns unit** – MDT (dermatology, ophthalmology, nutrition)
• Specific therapy (slide: **IV immunoglobulin**; ciclosporin also used) – evidence limited

cards.q: How do you **prevent recurrence** after SJS?
cards.a:
• Give a **drug-allergy alert card**; document in all records
• Advise **lifelong avoidance** of the culprit and structurally related drugs
• Report the **adverse drug reaction** to NPRA (MADRAC)
• Consider HLA screening for relatives before high-risk drugs

cards.q: What are the **complications and prognosis** of SJS/TEN?
cards.a:
• Acute: **sepsis** (commonest cause of death), fluid/electrolyte loss, hypothermia, respiratory involvement
• Long-term: **ocular scarring**, dry eye, **blindness**; nail loss, strictures
• Mortality ~**5–10% in SJS**, ~**30% or more in TEN**; severity scored with **SCORTEN**

cards.q: What is **Kawasaki disease (KD)**?
cards.a:
• An **acute systemic vasculitis** of **medium-sized arteries**
• Usually in children **<5 years**; more common in Asian children
• Aetiology **unknown** – likely an **infectious trigger** in genetically susceptible children

cards.q: What is the **most important complication** of Kawasaki disease?
cards.a:
• **Coronary artery aneurysm**
• → **thrombosis, acute myocardial infarction**, sudden death
• Leading cause of **acquired heart disease in children** in developed countries

cards.q: What are the **diagnostic criteria** for classic Kawasaki disease?
cards.a:
• **Fever for ≥5 days** (slide writes '>5 days'; standard criterion is ≥5 days)
• **PLUS ≥4 of the 5 CRASH** principal features
• Exclude look-alikes (measles, scarlet fever, TSS, drug reaction)
cards.m: 5 days of fever + 4 of 5 features.

cards.q: Expand the **CRASH and BURN** mnemonic.
cards.a:
• **C**onjunctivitis – **bilateral, non-purulent** (limbal sparing)
• **R**ash – **polymorphous**
• **A**denopathy – **unilateral cervical >1.5 cm**
• **S**trawberry tongue / oral mucosal changes (red cracked lips)
• **H**ands and feet – swelling, erythema, later desquamation
• **BURN** = fever (≥5 days)

cards.q: When can Kawasaki disease be diagnosed with **fewer than 4 criteria**?
cards.a:
• When **coronary artery abnormality** is shown on **echocardiography** in a child with prolonged fever
• Also the basis of **incomplete KD** diagnosis with supportive labs

cards.q: Describe the **three phases** of Kawasaki disease.
cards.a:
• **Acute (1–2 weeks):** fever, mucocutaneous signs
• **Subacute (2–4 weeks):** defervescence, **periungual desquamation**, **thrombocytosis**, **coronary aneurysm** formation
• **Convalescent (4–8 weeks):** signs resolve, inflammatory markers normalise
cards.m: Aneurysms and high platelets arrive as the fever leaves.

cards.q: What is **incomplete Kawasaki disease**, and who is at risk?
cards.a:
• Features suggestive of KD but **fewer than 4 principal criteria**
• Frequent in **infants <12 months**
• Delayed diagnosis → late treatment → **more coronary complications**
• Consider in any infant with **unexplained prolonged fever + raised inflammatory markers**; low threshold for echo
cards.m: The younger the baby, the fewer the signs, the bigger the risk.

cards.q: What **atypical presentations** of Kawasaki disease are described?
cards.a:
• **Acute abdomen**
• **Acute pancreatitis**
• **Cholestatic jaundice** (gallbladder hydrops)
• **Acute kidney injury**
• **Pneumonia**

cards.q: When is **echocardiography** done in Kawasaki disease?
cards.a:
• Transthoracic echo in **all suspected KD**
• **At diagnosis**
• At **2–3 weeks** after onset
• At **6–8 weeks** after onset
cards.m: Echo at 0, 2–3 and 6–8 weeks.

cards.q: Give the **IVIG** regimen for Kawasaki disease.
cards.a:
• **IVIG 2 g/kg single infusion over 10–12 hours**
• Start **as early as possible**, preferably **within 10 days** of onset
• Still give **after day 10** if persistent fever, coronary abnormality or ongoing inflammation (raised ESR/CRP)
• Divided lower doses may be used in sick infants who cannot tolerate volume
cards.m: 2 g/kg within 10 days.

cards.q: What is the **high-dose (anti-inflammatory) aspirin** regimen in Kawasaki disease?
cards.a:
• **30–50 mg/kg/day** in divided doses (Malaysian Paediatric Protocol)
• **Started together with IVIG**
• Continued until afebrile

cards.q: What is the **low-dose (antiplatelet) aspirin** regimen in Kawasaki disease?
cards.a:
• **3–5 mg/kg/day**
• Started **48–72 hours after defervescence**
• Continue **6–8 weeks** or until **ESR and platelet count normalise** (whichever is later) if no coronary abnormality
• **Coronary involvement:** continue until lesions resolve or **indefinitely**

cards.q: Why is aspirin used in Kawasaki disease despite the **Reye syndrome** rule, and what precautions follow?
cards.a:
• KD is the **key exception** – benefit (anti-inflammatory, antiplatelet) outweighs risk
• Reye risk rises with **influenza or varicella** while on aspirin
• Give **inactivated influenza vaccine**; review urgently if exposed to flu/chickenpox (may switch antiplatelet temporarily)
• Avoid **ibuprofen** – blocks aspirin’s antiplatelet effect

cards.q: How does **IVIG affect vaccination** after Kawasaki disease?
cards.a:
• IVIG antibodies **impair the response to live-attenuated viral vaccines** (MMR, varicella)
• **Delay live vaccines for at least 11 months** after IVIG
• Inactivated vaccines can be given on schedule
cards.m: IVIG = 11 months before MMR.

cards.q: How is a **giant coronary artery aneurysm** managed in KD?
cards.a:
• High risk of **acute coronary thrombosis**
• Add anticoagulation/extra antiplatelet to aspirin: **oral clopidogrel**, **oral warfarin**, **subcutaneous enoxaparin** or **IV heparin infusion**
• Long-term cardiology follow-up

cards.q: When should a GP **suspect Kawasaki disease** and what is the next step?
cards.a:
• Any young child with **fever ≥5 days** plus red eyes, red lips/tongue, rash, swollen hands/feet or neck node – especially if **not settling on antibiotics**
• Supportive labs: raised **CRP/ESR**, neutrophilia, **low albumin**, raised ALT, **sterile pyuria**, **thrombocytosis** after day 7
• → **Same-day paediatric referral** for echo and IVIG – do not start aspirin at the clinic

mcq.stem:
A 78-year-old woman is brought to the Klinik Kesihatan with 2 weeks of itchy skin. On her thighs and lower abdomen there are several tense, fluid-filled blisters measuring 15–20 mm on a red base. Mucous membranes are spared and the Nikolsky sign is negative. She is afebrile.
Which term most accurately describes the primary lesions?
mcq.e: Fluid-filled raised lesions are vesicles if <5 mm and bullae if >5 mm, so blisters of 15–20 mm are bullae. Tense bullae in an elderly patient with intact mucosa and a negative Nikolsky sign suggest bullous pemphigoid. The trap is calling every blister a vesicle – size is the discriminator.
w: Wrong - vesicles are fluid-filled blisters <5 mm, as in chickenpox or herpes simplex.
Wrong - pustules contain pus, not clear fluid, e.g. acne or folliculitis.
Correct - fluid-filled blisters larger than 5 mm are bullae; the classic example is bullous pemphigoid.
Wrong - wheals are transient oedematous swellings of urticaria with no fluid cavity.
Wrong - plaques are solid, palpable, plateau-like lesions (psoriasis, tinea), not fluid-filled.

mcq.stem:
A 6-year-old boy has had fever for 12 hours. His mother noticed small dark red spots on his shins. You press the side of a clear drinking glass firmly over the spots and they remain clearly visible through the glass.
What does this finding indicate about the spots?
o: Blood has leaked out of vessels into the skin
Dermal capillaries are dilated with increased flow
Fluid has collected in the dermis as oedema
Dead stratum corneum has heaped up on the surface
Dried serous exudate has formed on the surface
mcq.e: Erythema is due to capillary dilatation and blanches because pressure empties the vessels; purpura and petechiae are haemorrhage outside the vessels, so pressure cannot push the colour away. A non-blanching rash with fever must be treated as meningococcal septicaemia until proven otherwise.
w: Correct - non-blanching spots are extravasated blood (petechiae/purpura); with fever this is a red flag for meningococcaemia.
Wrong - capillary dilatation produces erythema, which blanches under the glass.
Wrong - dermal oedema produces wheals (urticaria), which also blanch.
Wrong - heaped-up stratum corneum is scale, a surface change, not a colour that persists under pressure.
Wrong - dried exudate is crust, e.g. on healing chickenpox lesions.

mcq.stem:
A 55-year-old man with long-standing psoriasis stopped his treatment 1 month ago. He now has bright red, mildly scaly skin over almost his entire body surface, with only small patches of normal skin left. He feels cold and is shivering; temperature 35.6°C, pulse 104/min.
Which descriptive term best fits this presentation?
mcq.e: Erythroderma is widespread reddening of more than 90% of the skin, usually due to an underlying inflammatory dermatosis such as psoriasis or eczema. Loss of skin barrier function causes heat and fluid loss, hypothermia and high-output strain, so it needs hospital referral. Scale may be present but does not describe the whole picture.
w: Wrong - urticaria is transient itchy wheals from dermal oedema, not fixed redness of the whole skin.
Wrong - purpura is non-blanching haemorrhage into the skin; this redness is inflammatory erythema.
Wrong - scaling is a surface change present here, but the defining feature is redness of >90% of the skin.
Wrong - lichenification is localised skin thickening from chronic rubbing, as in chronic eczema.
Correct - widespread reddening of >90% of the skin from inflammatory skin disease is erythroderma; urgent referral is needed.

mcq.stem:
A 30-year-old oil palm plantation worker presents with a 3-week history of an itchy lesion on his flank. It is a 4 cm ring with a raised, red, scaly advancing edge and a clear centre. Two smaller similar lesions are appearing nearby.
Which configuration and most likely cause fit best?
mcq.e: Annular lesions are rings with central clearing and an active edge; in a hot, humid occupation with itch and a scaly advancing border, tinea corporis is most likely. Nummular lesions are coin-shaped and uniformly involved without central clearing. Skin scrapings for KOH microscopy confirm the diagnosis.
w: Wrong - nummular means coin-shaped and uniformly involved, without central clearing.
Correct - a ring with central clearing and a scaly active edge is annular; tinea corporis is the classic cause.
Wrong - linear lesions follow straight lines, typically excoriations from scratching.
Wrong - gyrate lesions are wavy, curvilinear arcs; erythema annulare centrifugum is much less likely in this setting.
Wrong - psoriatic plaques are uniformly scaly discs without a clear centre.

mcq.stem:
A 28-year-old man who smokes 20 cigarettes a day attends the Klinik Kesihatan. Itchy vesicles appeared on his chest and back 18 hours ago and new crops are still appearing. He has fever 38.5°C, no cough or breathlessness, respiratory rate 16/min and SpO2 98% on air.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Calamine and antihistamine only, no antiviral
Oral ibuprofen for fever and review in 3 days
Refer for IV aciclovir for varicella pneumonia
Oral aciclovir 800 mg five times daily for 7 days
Oral co-amoxiclav to prevent secondary infection
mcq.e: Adults (and adolescents) have more severe varicella, and smokers have a higher risk of pneumonia, so oral aciclovir is indicated when started within 24 hours of rash onset (slide: within 24–48 hours of new vesicles). He has no features of pneumonia, so IV therapy is not needed yet. Symptomatic-only care is for healthy children or adults presenting >48 hours with no new lesions.
w: Wrong - symptomatic care alone suits healthy children; an adult smoker within 24 hours of rash benefits from an antiviral.
Wrong - NSAIDs are best avoided in varicella (invasive group A streptococcal infection) and the plan omits the antiviral.
Wrong - he has no cough, tachypnoea or hypoxia, so there is no evidence of pneumonia needing IV therapy.
Correct - an adult within 24 hours of rash onset, with smoking as an added risk factor, should receive oral aciclovir.
Wrong - prophylactic antibiotics are not indicated; treat secondary infection only if it develops.

mcq.stem:
A 6-year-old girl has had chickenpox for 4 days. She is afebrile and eating well, but a few new vesicles appeared this morning on her back; older lesions are crusting. Her mother asks when she can return to school.
What is the correct advice?
o: Once fever has settled for 24 hours
Once every lesion has crusted over
Seven days after the first exposure
Once the itch no longer needs treatment
Twenty-one days after the rash onset
mcq.e: Varicella is infectious from about 1–2 days before the rash until all lesions have crusted, because vesicle fluid contains live virus. New vesicles mean she is still infectious even though she is afebrile. Exclusion is usually about 5–7 days from rash onset; 21 days is the upper incubation period, not the infectious period.
w: Wrong - being afebrile does not end infectivity; fresh vesicles still shed virus.
Correct - the child remains infectious until every lesion has crusted, so she stays home until then.
Wrong - timing from exposure is irrelevant once she has the rash; infectivity depends on crusting.
Wrong - itch can continue after crusting and is not a marker of infectivity.
Wrong - 21 days is the upper limit of the incubation period, used for watching exposed contacts.

mcq.stem:
A 24-year-old woman at 16 weeks of gestation attends the Klinik Kesihatan. Her 5-year-old son developed chickenpox 2 days ago. She does not remember having chickenpox and has never been vaccinated. She is well with no rash.
What is the best next step?
o: Give live varicella vaccine within 3–5 days
Reassure, as second-trimester infection is harmless
Counsel her that termination is advisable
Isolate her son and review only if a rash appears
Urgent VZV IgG; give VZIG if she is non-immune
mcq.e: A pregnant woman with uncertain immunity after significant exposure should have urgent VZV IgG testing, and if non-immune she receives varicella-zoster immune globulin to attenuate infection. Varicella in pregnancy risks severe maternal pneumonia and, before 20 weeks, congenital varicella syndrome. The varicella vaccine is live and contraindicated in pregnancy.
w: Wrong - the varicella vaccine is live and contraindicated in pregnancy.
Wrong - maternal pneumonia is a real risk and fetal varicella syndrome can occur before 20 weeks.
Wrong - the absolute fetal risk is low (about 1–2%) and exposure alone is not an indication for termination.
Wrong - waiting for a rash misses the window for post-exposure prophylaxis.
Correct - confirm immunity urgently and give VZIG to a non-immune pregnant contact.

mcq.stem:
A 4-year-old boy with day 2 of chickenpox has a temperature of 38.8°C and is irritable. His mother has ibuprofen syrup, aspirin tablets and paracetamol syrup at home and asks which to use.
What is the most appropriate advice?
o: Paracetamol, avoiding both ibuprofen and aspirin
Aspirin, because it also helps to reduce the itch
Ibuprofen, alternating with aspirin every 4 hours
Ibuprofen alone, as it is the most effective option
Mefenamic acid, because it is gentle on the stomach
mcq.e: Aspirin in children with viral illnesses such as varicella or influenza can trigger Reye syndrome (encephalopathy with fatty liver failure). NSAIDs including ibuprofen are associated with severe invasive group A streptococcal skin and soft-tissue infection in varicella. Paracetamol is the antipyretic of choice.
w: Correct - paracetamol is safe; aspirin risks Reye syndrome and NSAIDs are linked to invasive streptococcal infection.
Wrong - aspirin in a child with varicella can trigger Reye syndrome and has no antipruritic role.
Wrong - this combines both drugs that should be avoided.
Wrong - ibuprofen is linked with severe invasive group A streptococcal infection in varicella.
Wrong - mefenamic acid is also an NSAID and offers no advantage.

mcq.stem:
A 5-year-old girl had chickenpox 9 days ago and her lesions have crusted. Today she walks with a wide-based, unsteady gait and falls easily. She is alert, smiling and afebrile, with no headache, vomiting or neck stiffness. Examination shows nystagmus and intention tremor; power and reflexes are normal.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcq.e: Acute cerebellar ataxia is the commonest neurological complication of varicella in children, typically about a week after the rash, with ataxia and nystagmus in an alert child; it is usually self-limiting. Encephalitis causes reduced consciousness, seizures or fever. Guillain-Barré causes weakness with lost reflexes rather than cerebellar signs.
w: Wrong - encephalitis causes drowsiness, confusion or seizures; this child is alert.
Wrong - Reye syndrome causes vomiting and encephalopathy with liver failure, usually after aspirin.
Correct - isolated cerebellar signs in an alert child about a week after chickenpox is acute cerebellar ataxia.
Wrong - Guillain-Barré causes ascending weakness with areflexia, not nystagmus and intention tremor.
Wrong - she has no fever, headache or meningism.

mcq.stem:
A 32-year-old man who smokes is on day 3 of chickenpox. Since last night he has a dry cough and breathlessness. Temperature 38.9°C, respiratory rate 28/min, SpO2 91% on air, scattered crackles in both lungs.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Oral aciclovir and review in 24 hours
Oral amoxicillin and outpatient chest X-ray
Nebulised salbutamol and a course of prednisolone
Oxygen and urgent referral for IV aciclovir
mcq.e: Varicella pneumonia is the most important serious complication in adults, especially smokers, pregnant women and the immunocompromised, and usually appears 1–6 days after the rash. Tachypnoea and hypoxia mean he needs oxygen and urgent hospital transfer for IV aciclovir. Oral therapy and outpatient review are unsafe once pneumonia is present.
w: Wrong - oral aciclovir is not adequate once hypoxic pneumonia has developed.
Wrong - this is viral pneumonitis needing IV antiviral; outpatient care is unsafe with SpO2 91%.
Wrong - steroids are not first-line and may worsen viral infection; this is not asthma.
Correct - hypoxic varicella pneumonia needs oxygen and urgent transfer for IV aciclovir.
Wrong - symptomatic care ignores a life-threatening complication.

mcq.stem:
A 7-year-old boy who received two doses of varicella vaccine develops about 30 itchy lesions on his trunk, mostly red papules with only a few small vesicles. Temperature 37.6°C. His younger sister is 4 months old.
What is the most appropriate advice to his parents?
o: He is still contagious and should stay off school
He cannot be infectious as he is fully vaccinated
Vaccine failure means he needs a third dose soon
Such mild lesions must be due to insect bites
He needs oral aciclovir as vaccinated cases relapse
mcq.e: Breakthrough varicella is wild-type infection more than 42 days after vaccination; it is milder (afebrile or low-grade fever, usually <50 mainly maculopapular lesions) but still contagious. He should be kept from school and away from the young infant until no new lesions appear and existing ones have crusted or faded. Antivirals are not routinely needed for a healthy child.
w: Correct - breakthrough varicella is mild but contagious, so he needs exclusion and should avoid his infant sister.
Wrong - vaccinated children with breakthrough disease can transmit the virus.
Wrong - a further dose is not part of management of an active breakthrough infection.
Wrong - mild, few-lesion disease with low-grade fever after vaccination is typical of breakthrough varicella.
Wrong - healthy children do not need antivirals, and relapse is not a feature.

mcq.stem:
A 20-year-old female nursing student had prolonged face-to-face contact with a patient with chickenpox 2 days ago. Her VZV IgG is negative. She is healthy, not pregnant and takes no medication.
What is the most appropriate post-exposure measure?
o: Reassurance only, as adults rarely become ill
Oral aciclovir for 7 days, starting immediately
Varicella vaccine within 3–5 days of exposure
mcq.e: For healthy, non-immune, non-pregnant contacts, varicella vaccine within 3–5 days of exposure can prevent or modify disease and gives future immunity.
