VZIG is reserved for high-risk contacts in whom live vaccine is contraindicated: immunocompromised people, non-immune pregnant women and newborns. Adults get more severe varicella, so reassurance alone is wrong.
w: Wrong - VZIG is for high-risk contacts (immunocompromised, pregnant, neonates), not healthy adults.
Wrong - adults have more severe disease and higher pneumonia risk than children.
Wrong - immediate antiviral prophylaxis is not the standard measure for a healthy contact.
Correct - healthy non-immune contacts should be vaccinated within 3–5 days of exposure.
Wrong - normal human immunoglobulin is used for measles exposure, not varicella.

mcq.stem:
A woman develops a typical chickenpox rash 2 days before an uncomplicated term vaginal delivery. Her baby boy is well at birth, feeding and afebrile. The mother asks what will be done for the baby.
What is the most appropriate management for the newborn?
o: Reassure, as maternal antibodies protect the baby
Give VZIG to the newborn and observe closely
Delay breastfeeding until the mother's lesions crust
Discharge home and review only if fever develops
mcq.e: When maternal rash appears from 5 days before to 2 days after delivery, the baby is exposed to virus before protective maternal IgG has crossed the placenta, so severe neonatal varicella can occur. The newborn should receive VZIG promptly and be watched closely, with IV aciclovir if lesions develop. Breastfeeding can usually continue.
w: Wrong - the live vaccine is not used in newborns and would not act quickly enough.
Wrong - maternal IgG takes about 5–7 days to form and cross the placenta, so this baby is unprotected.
Correct - babies of mothers with rash from 5 days before to 2 days after delivery need VZIG and close observation.
Wrong - breastfeeding is not contraindicated and stopping it does not prevent infection.
Wrong - neonatal varicella can be severe and progress quickly; prophylaxis should not be withheld.

mcq.stem:
A 2-year-old unvaccinated girl has had fever, cough, runny nose and red watery eyes for 4 days. Today a blotchy red maculopapular rash started on her face and behind her ears and is spreading to the trunk. She looks miserable. Tiny white specks are seen on a red buccal mucosa opposite the molars.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcq.e: Fever with the 3 Cs (cough, coryza, conjunctivitis) for a few days, followed by a rash starting on the face and behind the ears and spreading downwards, is classic measles. Koplik spots (white grains on the buccal mucosa) are pathognomonic. Rubella is milder, with postauricular nodes and no Koplik spots.
w: Wrong - in roseola the rash appears as the fever settles, starts on the trunk and the child is well.
Wrong - scarlet fever has a sandpaper rash with sore throat and strawberry tongue, not the 3 Cs.
Wrong - Kawasaki conjunctivitis is non-exudative and dry, with no coryza, cough or Koplik spots.
Wrong - rubella is a mild illness with postauricular lymphadenopathy and no Koplik spots.
Correct - the 3 Cs, Koplik spots and a cephalocaudal rash are diagnostic of measles.

mcq.stem:
A Klinik Kesihatan doctor sees a 3-year-old with fever, maculopapular rash, cough and conjunctivitis. Throat swab and serum have been taken; results will take several days.
Which public health action is correct?
o: Notify within 7 days once serology is positive
Notify within 24 hours, before any results
Notify only if a second linked case appears
Notify within 24 hours of a positive RT-PCR
Notify within 1 week after the rash has faded
mcq.e: The child meets the clinical case definition of measles (fever, maculopapular rash and cough/coryza/conjunctivitis), so notification to the District Health Office is required within 24 hours of clinical diagnosis. Waiting for laboratory results delays contact tracing and outbreak vaccination under the measles elimination programme.
w: Wrong - measles is a 24-hour notification and does not wait for serology.
Correct - a clinically suspected measles case is notified within 24 hours without waiting for results.
Wrong - a single suspected case must be notified.
Wrong - notification is based on clinical suspicion, not laboratory confirmation.
Wrong - the 7-day window applies to diseases such as typhoid and typhus, not measles.

mcq.stem:
A 14-month-old boy weighing 10 kg is diagnosed with measles on day 5 of illness. He is drinking adequately, has no respiratory distress and no eye signs.
Which vitamin A regimen is recommended?
mcq.e: WHO recommends vitamin A for all children with measles as two doses 24 hours apart: 50 000 IU under 6 months, 100 000 IU at 6–11 months and 200 000 IU from 12 months. It reduces severe complications and death, especially in malnourished children. A third dose is given 2–4 weeks later if there are eye signs of deficiency.
w: Wrong - 50 000 IU is the dose for infants under 6 months, and two doses are needed.
Wrong - 100 000 IU is the dose for 6–11 months, and it is given twice.
Wrong - this is the correct regimen for 6–11 months, but he is 14 months old.
Wrong - the dose is right for his age but a second dose 24 hours later is required.
Correct - children aged 12 months or more receive 200 000 IU on two consecutive days.

mcq.stem:
A 9-year-old boy presents on day 2 of a maculopapular rash that began behind the ears, after 3 days of fever, cough and conjunctivitis. You want laboratory confirmation for the health office.
Which specimen is preferred?
o: Serum measles IgG on the first day of rash
Nasopharyngeal or throat swab for RT-PCR
Blood culture taken before any antibiotic
Paired sera taken 6 weeks apart for IgM
Punch biopsy taken from an area of rash
mcq.e: Measles is confirmed by RT-PCR, for which nasopharyngeal or throat swabs are the preferred specimens (urine or blood can also be used), and by serum measles-specific IgM in the first days of the rash. IgG indicates past infection or vaccination and is not diagnostic of acute illness.
w: Wrong - IgG shows past infection or vaccination; IgM or PCR is needed for acute diagnosis.
Correct - a nasopharyngeal or throat swab for RT-PCR is the preferred confirmatory specimen.
Wrong - measles is viral; blood culture has no role in confirming it.
Wrong - IgM is detected within the first few days of rash; waiting 6 weeks is unnecessary and too late for public health action.
Wrong - skin biopsy is not used to diagnose measles.

mcq.stem:
An 11-year-old boy is brought in because his school performance has declined over 6 months, with personality change and recent sudden jerking movements of his limbs. He had measles at 1 year of age and has no other history.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcq.e: SSPE is a rare, fatal progressive encephalitis due to persistent measles virus, appearing about 7–10 years after measles, with higher risk if infection occurred before 2 years of age. It presents with intellectual and behavioural decline followed by myoclonic jerks and dementia. Measles vaccination prevents it.
w: Wrong - ADEM is an acute illness days to weeks after an infection, not a slow decline years later.
Wrong - juvenile myoclonic epilepsy causes morning myoclonus without progressive cognitive decline.
Wrong - Wilson disease can cause neuropsychiatric change but the measles history and myoclonus point elsewhere.
Correct - progressive decline and myoclonus years after early measles is SSPE.
Wrong - ADHD is a developmental condition and does not cause new myoclonic jerks.

mcq.stem:
A 3-year-old unvaccinated girl spent the afternoon playing with a cousin who was diagnosed with measles the next day. The contact was 48 hours ago. She is well and has no immunodeficiency.
What is the most appropriate action?
o: Give MMR now, within 72 hours of exposure
Give vitamin A prophylaxis and observe
Wait and vaccinate at the next routine visit
Start oral ribavirin as post-exposure cover
mcq.e: A susceptible contact aged 6 months or older should receive MMR within 72 hours of exposure, which can prevent or modify measles and completes her overdue vaccination. Normal human immunoglobulin within 6 days is reserved for high-risk contacts who cannot have a live vaccine, such as infants under 6 months, non-immune pregnant women and the immunocompromised.
w: Correct - MMR within 72 hours protects a healthy susceptible contact and catches up her immunisation.
Wrong - immunoglobulin is for high-risk contacts unable to receive live vaccine.
Wrong - vitamin A is given to children with measles, not as prophylaxis for contacts.
Wrong - delaying vaccination misses the 72-hour post-exposure window.
Wrong - ribavirin is not used for measles post-exposure prophylaxis.

mcq.stem:
An 18-month-old malnourished child is on day 6 of measles. The fever had begun to settle but has returned. He now has a respiratory rate of 58/min, subcostal recession and crackles at both lung bases.
Which complication is this, and which is the commonest cause of death from measles?
mcq.e: Bronchopneumonia, viral or secondary bacterial, is the commonest serious complication and the leading cause of death in measles, particularly in malnourished, vitamin A-deficient children. Recurrence of fever after initial improvement with tachypnoea suggests secondary bacterial infection, needing admission and antibiotics. Encephalitis is rarer and presents with altered consciousness or seizures.
w: Wrong - encephalitis is serious but less common and presents with drowsiness or seizures.
Wrong - otitis media is common but rarely fatal and does not cause tachypnoea with crackles.
Correct - recurrent fever with tachypnoea and crackles is bronchopneumonia, the main cause of measles deaths.
Wrong - myocarditis is a rare complication and would not explain the chest signs.
Wrong - keratitis causes eye pain and blindness risk, not respiratory distress.

mcq.stem:
An 11-month-old boy had a temperature up to 40.2°C for 4 days, yet remained playful and fed well. The fever settled yesterday and this morning a pink, blanching maculopapular rash appeared on his trunk and upper limbs, sparing the face. There is mild cervical lymphadenopathy; no conjunctivitis, cough or mouth changes.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcq.e: Roseola (HHV-6) classically causes 3–5 days of high fever in a surprisingly well infant aged 6 months to 2 years, followed by a blanching rash on the trunk as the fever settles. The key discriminator is timing: the rash appears after defervescence. Measles and Kawasaki rashes appear while the fever is ongoing.
w: Wrong - in measles the child is ill with the 3 Cs and the rash appears at the height of fever, starting on the face.
Wrong - rubella has low-grade fever with the rash starting on the face, not after 4 days of high fever.
Wrong - scarlet fever has a sandpaper rash with sore throat and is uncommon in infants.
Correct - high fever for several days in a well infant, then a truncal rash once the fever settles, is roseola.
Wrong - Kawasaki needs fever of 5 or more days with mucocutaneous signs; the fever does not end before the rash.

mcq.stem:
A 13-month-old girl was given amoxicillin by a private clinic on day 3 of a high fever without a source. On day 4 the fever settled and a pink, blanching rash appeared on her trunk. She is well and feeding normally. Her mother is worried that the girl is allergic to penicillin.
What is the most appropriate advice?
o: Record a lifelong penicillin allergy in her notes
Explain it is a viral rash, not a drug allergy
Start oral prednisolone and an antihistamine
Refer urgently to dermatology for patch testing
Admit for observation and intravenous fluids
mcq.e: The roseola rash commonly appears after an antibiotic has been started for the unexplained fever, and is then mislabelled as a drug allergy. Recognising the fever-then-rash pattern avoids a false lifelong penicillin allergy label. Management is reassurance, paracetamol and fluids.
w: Wrong - a false allergy label would deprive her of first-line antibiotics for life.
Correct - this is the typical roseola sequence; reassure and do not label her as penicillin-allergic.
Wrong - the rash is benign and fades within 1–2 days without treatment.
Wrong - no testing is needed for a self-limiting viral exanthem.
Wrong - a well child who is feeding normally does not need admission.

mcq.stem:
A 14-month-old boy has a temperature of 40.1°C on day 2 of illness with no rash and no focus on examination. At home he had a generalised tonic-clonic seizure lasting 3 minutes; he is now alert and playful. There is no family history of epilepsy.
Which virus is the most common cause of this pattern in this age group?
mcq.e: Primary HHV-6 infection (roseola) causes abrupt high fever in infants aged 6 months to 2 years and is an important cause of febrile seizures, which occur during the febrile phase before the rash. Most are simple seizures needing only reassurance. Parvovirus B19 causes slapped cheek with little fever.
w: Correct - HHV-6 (roseola) commonly causes high fever with febrile seizures in infants before any rash appears.
Wrong - EV71 causes HFMD with oral ulcers and hand–foot lesions; neurological disease looks different (myoclonus, lethargy).
Wrong - measles has a prominent prodrome of cough, coryza and conjunctivitis.
Wrong - varicella presents with an itchy vesicular rash, not isolated high fever.
Wrong - parvovirus B19 causes erythema infectiosum with mild fever.

mcq.stem:
Several infants with presumed roseola are seen at a Klinik Kesihatan on the same day.
Which finding is an indication for hospital referral?
o: Pink rash appearing as the fever settles
mcq.e: Roseola is usually managed at home with reassurance, paracetamol and fluids. Referral is needed for complex febrile seizures (focal, longer than 15 minutes or recurrent within 24 hours), status epilepticus, prolonged lethargy or signs of secondary bacterial infection. High fever, the rash and mild lymphadenopathy are expected features.
w: Wrong - fever above 40°C is typical of roseola and not on its own a referral criterion.
Wrong - a rash after defervescence is the expected course of roseola.
Wrong - mild cervical lymphadenopathy is a recognised benign feature.
Wrong - mild anorexia with adequate fluid intake can be managed at home.
Correct - a focal seizure lasting more than 15 minutes is a complex febrile seizure and needs referral.

mcq.stem:
A 3-year-old girl from a kindergarten where other children are unwell has had fever for 1 day and is refusing food because of mouth pain. There are shallow ulcers on her tongue and buccal mucosa, and oval greyish vesicles on her palms, soles and buttocks. The lesions are not itchy.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcq.e: HFMD causes fever with painful oral ulcers and flat or oval vesicles on the palms, soles, buttocks and genital area in children under 5 years, often in nursery outbreaks. Herpangina affects only the posterior pharynx and soft palate without hand–foot lesions. Varicella is itchy and centripetal.
w: Wrong - varicella vesicles are itchy, in crops on the trunk, and do not localise to palms and soles.
Wrong - herpangina causes vesicles on the soft palate and posterior pharynx without skin lesions.
Correct - oral ulcers plus non-itchy vesicles on palms, soles and buttocks in a toddler are typical of HFMD.
Wrong - herpetic gingivostomatitis causes swollen bleeding gums and perioral vesicles, not palmar–plantar lesions.
Wrong - scarlet fever has a sandpaper rash and exudative tonsillitis, not vesicles.

mcq.stem:
A 2-year-old boy is on day 3 of HFMD. His mother says he has become sleepier and keeps startling with sudden jerks of his arms when falling asleep. Temperature 38.5°C, heart rate 170/min, capillary refill 2 seconds.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Same-day referral to hospital for admission
Paracetamol and review at the clinic in 48 hours
Oral rehydration at home with daily phone review
Oral aciclovir and review at the clinic tomorrow
Reassure that sleep jerks are common with fever
mcq.e: Increasing lethargy and myoclonic jerks are neurological danger signs of severe enterovirus (especially EV71) infection, which can progress within hours to brainstem encephalitis, pulmonary oedema and cardiopulmonary collapse. Tachycardia out of proportion to fever adds concern. He must be referred to hospital urgently.
w: Correct - myoclonic jerks, lethargy and tachycardia are danger signs requiring urgent hospital admission.
Wrong - deterioration with EV71 can occur within hours, so a 48-hour review is unsafe.
Wrong - home care is inappropriate once neurological danger signs appear.
Wrong - aciclovir has no activity against enteroviruses.
Wrong - myoclonic jerks in HFMD are a warning sign, not a benign feature of fever.

mcq.stem:
A Klinik Kesihatan doctor sees a 4-year-old with fever, oral ulcers and vesicles on the palms and soles. A throat swab for enterovirus has been sent and the result will take a week.
Which statement about notification is correct?
o: Notify only after the viral PCR is positive
Notify within 7 days of the clinical diagnosis
Notify within 24 hours as a suspected case
Notify only if another child in the class is ill
No notification is needed if the case is mild
mcq.e: HFMD must be notified to the District Health Office within 24 hours of a suspected case, and laboratory confirmation is not required. Early notification allows outbreak control measures at the kindergarten or nursery, including closure if needed.
w: Wrong - laboratory confirmation is not required before notifying HFMD.
Wrong - HFMD is a 24-hour notification; 7 days applies to diseases such as typhoid and typhus.
Correct - a suspected HFMD case is notified within 24 hours without waiting for results.
Wrong - a single suspected case is notifiable.
Wrong - severity does not change the duty to notify.

mcq.stem:
An 18-month-old boy with oral ulcers and palmar vesicles for 2 days is now pale, with cold peripheries, heart rate 190/min, capillary refill 4 seconds, a gallop rhythm and fine crackles at both lung bases.
Which virus is most likely responsible for this severe course?
mcq.e: EV71 causes the severe and fatal forms of HFMD seen in Malaysian outbreaks: brainstem encephalitis leading to neurogenic pulmonary oedema and cardiopulmonary failure. Coxsackievirus A16 is the commonest cause but usually mild. Signs of cardiac involvement need immediate resuscitation and transfer.
w: Wrong - coxsackievirus A16 is the commonest cause of HFMD but typically causes mild illness.
Wrong - echoviruses can cause HFMD-like illness but are not the classic cause of severe disease.
Wrong - polioviruses are enteroviruses but do not cause HFMD (the slide listing is a slip).
Wrong - HSV causes gingivostomatitis, not palmar–plantar vesicles with cardiopulmonary failure.
Correct - EV71 causes severe neurological and cardiopulmonary HFMD with deaths.

mcq.stem:
A 4-year-old girl with HFMD has been afebrile since day 3. On day 5 there are still several intact vesicles on her hands and feet, but she is eating well. Her mother wants to send her back to kindergarten tomorrow.
What is the correct advice?
o: Return now as fever has settled for a day
Return after a full course of antibiotics
Return once the mouth ulcers stop hurting
Keep home until all blisters have healed
Keep home for 21 days from rash onset
mcq.e: Children with HFMD remain infectious until the blisters have ruptured and healed, usually 7–10 days, because vesicle fluid contains virus. She should stay away from kindergarten until then. Virus is shed in stool for weeks afterwards, so hand hygiene must continue after return.
w: Wrong - being afebrile does not end infectivity while vesicles remain.
Wrong - HFMD is viral and antibiotics play no role.
Wrong - pain relief does not mean the skin lesions have stopped shedding virus.
Correct - she is infectious until the blisters have ruptured and healed, usually 7–10 days.
Wrong - 21 days is unnecessarily long; exclusion is based on healing of the blisters.

mcq.stem:
During a nursery outbreak, five children with HFMD are seen at a Klinik Kesihatan.
Which child can safely be managed at home?
o: A child refusing all fluids with no urine for 8 hours
A child with ulcers who is drinking well and playful
A child whose fever above 39°C has lasted 3 days
A child who is vomiting persistently and is lethargic
A child whose single mother says she cannot cope
mcq.e: Uncomplicated HFMD is managed at home with reassurance, paracetamol, adequate fluids and teaching of danger signs. Admission criteria include inability to tolerate oral fluids, hyperpyrexia persisting more than 48 hours, neurological or cardiac signs, a toxic appearance, and parents unable to cope or inadequate social support.
w: Wrong - inability to tolerate oral feeds with oliguria means dehydration risk and needs admission.
Correct - a playful child who is drinking well with only oral ulcers can be managed at home.
Wrong - hyperpyrexia persisting more than 48 hours is an admission criterion.
Wrong - persistent vomiting with lethargy suggests CNS involvement and requires admission.
Wrong - parents unable to cope or inadequate social support is an admission criterion.

mcq.stem:
A kindergarten teacher attends a Klinik Kesihatan health talk after three children in her class developed HFMD. She asks for practical prevention advice.
Which advice is most appropriate?
o: Prick the blisters so that they dry out faster
Children may share cups once their fever settles
Wash hands with soap after nappy changes for weeks
Hand sanitiser alone removes the need to clean toys
Apply antiseptic spray to the blisters twice daily
mcq.e: Enteroviruses spread by respiratory secretions, vesicle fluid and the faecal–oral route, and virus is shed in stool for several weeks after recovery. Hand washing with soap and water, disinfecting toys and surfaces, not sharing personal items and not rupturing blisters are the key measures.
w: Wrong - rupturing blisters releases virus-laden fluid and increases spread.
Wrong - personal items should not be shared; saliva remains infectious after fever settles.
Correct - faecal shedding continues for weeks, so soap-and-water hand washing after nappy changes is essential.
Wrong - toys and surfaces still need cleaning and disinfection; sanitiser is less effective than soap and water.
Wrong - antiseptic on blisters does not reduce transmission.

mcq.stem:
A 30-year-old man from a dengue hotspot in Petaling Jaya presents on day 2 of high fever with severe myalgia, headache and retro-orbital pain. He is drinking well and vital signs are stable.
Which test is most useful to confirm the diagnosis today?
mcq.e: NS1 antigen is detectable from day 1 to about day 5 of fever, so it is the test of choice early in the febrile phase. IgM appears from about day 5 (slides: primary infection day 6–10), so it is often negative on day 2. The tourniquet test only supports capillary fragility and does not confirm dengue.
w: Wrong - IgM usually appears from about day 5 and is often negative on day 2.
Wrong - IgG indicates past or secondary infection and does not confirm acute primary dengue early.
Wrong - the tourniquet test is supportive only and a negative result does not exclude dengue.
Wrong - Weil-Felix is a non-specific test for rickettsial infection (typhus).
Correct - NS1 antigen is positive in the early febrile phase (days 1–5).

mcq.stem:
A 25-year-old woman with NS1-positive dengue attends her daily review on day 5. Her fever settled this morning and she feels better, but has mild abdominal pain. Haematocrit has risen from 39% to 47% and platelets have fallen from 140 to 45 × 10⁹/L over 24 hours. BP 110/80 mmHg.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Discharge to work as the fever has resolved
Home care with repeat FBC in 48 hours
mcq.e: Defervescence around days 3–7 marks the start of the critical phase, when plasma leakage may cause shock even though the patient feels better. A rising haematocrit with a rapid fall in platelets, plus abdominal pain (a warning sign), are criteria for admission. Prophylactic platelet transfusion and steroids have no role.
w: Wrong - defervescence is the most dangerous time in dengue, not a sign of recovery.
Correct - rising HCT with falling platelets and abdominal pain mean plasma leakage; she must be admitted.
Wrong - she has a warning sign and haemoconcentration; a 48-hour delay could miss shock.
Wrong - prophylactic platelet transfusion is not recommended in stable patients without bleeding.
Wrong - steroids have no proven benefit in dengue.

mcq.stem:
A 22-year-old male student presents on day 3 of fever with a positive NS1. He is drinking well and passing urine normally, with no abdominal pain, vomiting or bleeding. BP 118/76 mmHg, pulse 88/min, capillary refill <2 seconds. HCT 42% (stable), platelets 130 × 10⁹/L. He has no comorbidities.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Home care with daily review and FBC
Home care, return only if he bleeds
mcq.e: Patients tolerating oral fluids, with stable vital signs, stable serial HCT, no warning signs, no bleeding and no comorbidity or pregnancy can be managed at home. They need daily clinical review with FBC from day 3 because the critical phase usually begins around days 3–7. Bleeding is only one of several warning signs.
w: Correct - he meets the outpatient criteria and needs daily review with FBC through the critical phase.
Wrong - IV fluids are not needed when he is drinking well with stable vital signs.
Wrong - waiting for bleeding misses silent plasma leakage; daily review is required from day 3.
Wrong - NSAIDs are avoided in dengue and a 3-day gap crosses the critical phase.
Wrong - admission criteria are not met; platelet count alone does not decide admission.

mcq.stem:
A 29-year-old woman at 24 weeks of gestation presents on day 3 of fever with a positive dengue NS1. She is drinking well, has no warning signs, BP 112/70 mmHg, pulse 90/min, HCT 36% and platelets 150 × 10⁹/L.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Home care with daily review from day 3
Home care with a review on day 5 only
Admit only if platelets fall below 50
Admit to hospital for monitoring now
Home care with daily phone follow-up
mcq.e: Pregnancy is a special risk group in the MOH dengue CPG, as are the elderly and patients with comorbidities, so she should be admitted even without warning signs. Pregnancy also masks haemoconcentration and shock, because of physiological haemodilution and tachycardia.
w: Wrong - this suits a low-risk non-pregnant adult; pregnancy is an admission criterion.
Wrong - a single review on day 5 is unsafe in any dengue patient, especially in pregnancy.
Wrong - admission is based on her risk group, not on a platelet threshold.
Correct - pregnant women with dengue meet the special-risk admission criteria.
Wrong - telephone follow-up cannot detect plasma leakage and is unsafe here.

mcq.stem:
A 35-year-old man with NS1-positive dengue on day 2 is managed as an outpatient. He has severe myalgia and headache and asks for an injection to relieve the pain quickly. He has no allergies.
Which analgesic plan is most appropriate?
o: Oral paracetamol, max 4 g per day
Oral mefenamic acid 500 mg three times daily
Oral aspirin 300 mg four times daily
mcq.e: Paracetamol is the only recommended analgesic and antipyretic in dengue. NSAIDs and aspirin impair platelet function and cause gastritis and bleeding, and intramuscular injections cause haematomas in thrombocytopenic patients. Tepid sponging can be added for fever.
w: Wrong - this combines an NSAID with an intramuscular injection, both avoided in dengue.
Correct - paracetamol within the maximum daily dose is the safe choice.
Wrong - mefenamic acid is an NSAID and increases bleeding risk.
Wrong - aspirin is an antiplatelet drug and is contraindicated in dengue.
Wrong - naproxen is an NSAID and is avoided in dengue.

mcq.stem:
A 27-year-old woman with confirmed dengue is reviewed on day 4 of illness at a Klinik Kesihatan. Her blood pressure is 116/78 mmHg and she is drinking well.
Which single finding is a dengue warning sign requiring admission?
o: Tender liver 3 cm below the costal margin
mcq.e: MOH CPG warning signs are abdominal pain or tenderness, persistent vomiting, clinical fluid accumulation, mucosal bleeding, lethargy or restlessness, tender liver enlargement more than 2 cm, and a rising HCT with a rapid fall in platelets. Headache, myalgia, flushing, high fever and a modest fall in platelets are expected febrile-phase features.
w: Wrong - mild thrombocytopenia alone is expected and is not a warning sign.
Wrong - retro-orbital headache and myalgia are typical febrile-phase symptoms.
Wrong - flushing and arthralgia are expected features of the febrile phase.
Correct - liver enlargement of more than 2 cm with tenderness is a warning sign needing admission.
Wrong - high fever is typical of the febrile phase and is not itself a warning sign.

mcq.stem:
A 40-year-old man presents on day 7 of a febrile illness with myalgia and a falling platelet count. A rapid combo test shows NS1 negative and IgM positive. He had no fever in the past year.
What is the best interpretation?
o: Dengue is likely; NS1 wanes after day 5
Dengue is excluded as the NS1 is negative
A false-positive IgM; repeat the NS1 now
Evidence of a dengue infection years ago
mcq.e: NS1 is detectable mainly in the first 5 days and often becomes negative later, while IgM rises from about day 5. A negative NS1 with positive IgM on day 7 is therefore consistent with current dengue. Interpreting tests according to the day of illness is the key skill.
w: Correct - by day 7 NS1 often becomes negative and IgM is positive, supporting current dengue.
Wrong - a negative NS1 after day 5 does not exclude dengue.
Wrong - there is no reason to suspect a false positive; repeating NS1 late adds nothing.
Wrong - IgM indicates recent infection; past infection is shown by IgG.
Wrong - there is no vaccination history to explain a positive IgM.

mcq.stem:
A 32-year-old man admitted with dengue is on day 8 of illness. His appetite has returned, he is passing large volumes of urine and has an itchy rash described as 'isles of white in a sea of red'. He is still receiving IV fluids at 3 ml/kg/h. He is now breathless with bilateral basal crackles; HCT has fallen to 36%.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Increase IV fluids for ongoing leakage
Stop IV fluids and consider a diuretic
IV hydrocortisone for the itchy rash
mcq.e: Return of appetite, diuresis, a falling HCT and the convalescent rash mark the recovery phase, when leaked fluid is reabsorbed. Continuing IV fluids now causes fluid overload and pulmonary oedema, so fluids should be stopped or tapered, with a diuretic if overloaded.
w: Wrong - leakage has stopped; extra fluid will worsen pulmonary oedema.
Wrong - the problem is fluid overload, not bleeding.
Correct - in the recovery phase IV fluids are stopped or tapered and a diuretic is considered for overload.
Wrong - the convalescent rash is benign and does not need steroids.
Wrong - the picture of recovery with diuresis and crackles is fluid overload, not pneumonia.

mcq.stem:
A 38-year-old woman (height 162 cm, weight 90 kg, BMI 34.3 kg/m²) is admitted with dengue and needs maintenance IV fluids. Following the MOH CPG, you calculate the body weight to use.
Which body weight should be used for her maintenance fluid calculation?
mcq.e: In obese patients (BMI >27.5 kg/m²) the CPG uses adjusted body weight. Ideal body weight for a woman = 45.5 + 0.91 × (162 − 152) = 54.6 kg; adjusted body weight = 54.6 + 0.4 × (90 − 54.6) = 68.8 kg. Using actual weight would overload her; using ideal weight would under-hydrate her.
w: Wrong - actual body weight overestimates fluid needs in obesity and risks overload.
Wrong - this is her ideal body weight; the CPG adds 40% of the excess weight.
Wrong - this is the simple average of actual and ideal weight, not the CPG formula.
Wrong - this adds only 20% of the excess weight; the CPG uses 0.4.
Correct - adjusted body weight = IBW 54.6 + 0.4 × (90 − 54.6) = 68.8 kg.

mcq.stem:
A 19-year-old man with NS1-positive dengue is managed at home and is on day 4 of illness. Before he leaves the Klinik Kesihatan you explain the dengue home care card.
Which symptom should make him return to the clinic immediately?
o: Itchy rash on the legs with white patches
Increased appetite and passing more urine
Slow pulse of 56/min while feeling well
No urine passed in the last 6 hours
mcq.e: The home care card tells patients to return at once for warning symptoms: abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, bleeding, drowsiness or restlessness, cold clammy limbs, or no urine for 4–6 hours, which suggests shock from plasma leakage. An itchy 'isles of white' rash, improving appetite, diuresis and relative bradycardia are features of recovery.
w: Wrong - the itchy convalescent rash is a sign of recovery.
Wrong - mild headache controlled by paracetamol is expected in the febrile phase.
Wrong - returning appetite and diuresis indicate the recovery phase.
Wrong - bradycardia in a well patient is a recognised recovery-phase finding.
Correct - no urine for 4–6 hours suggests hypovolaemia from plasma leakage and needs urgent review.

mcq.stem:
A 26-year-old woman on day 3 of fever has a blood pressure of 120/80 mmHg. A tourniquet test is performed with the cuff inflated to 100 mmHg for 5 minutes. Afterwards 25 petechiae are counted in a 2.5 cm × 2.5 cm square on the forearm.
How should this result be interpreted?
o: Negative; positive needs more than 50 petechiae
Invalid; the cuff should be held at systolic pressure
Positive; supports capillary fragility in dengue
Positive; confirms dengue and excludes other causes
Negative; the cuff must stay inflated for 10 minutes
mcq.e: The tourniquet test is done with the cuff midway between systolic and diastolic pressure for 5 minutes; 10 or more petechiae in a 2.5 cm square is positive. A positive result supports capillary fragility in dengue, but it is not diagnostic, and a negative result does not exclude dengue.
w: Wrong - the threshold is 10 or more petechiae per 2.5 cm square.
Wrong - the cuff is correctly held midway between systolic and diastolic pressure (100 mmHg).
Correct - 25 petechiae is a positive test supporting capillary fragility, consistent with dengue.
Wrong - a positive tourniquet test is supportive, not confirmatory; NS1 or serology confirms dengue.
Wrong - the standard inflation time is 5 minutes.

mcq.stem:
A 45-year-old oil palm plantation worker in Pahang has had fever, chills, headache, myalgia and a dry cough for 6 days. Examination shows a painless black crusted lesion with a red rim in his left groin, tender inguinal lymph nodes and a maculopapular rash on the trunk.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcq.e: An eschar (painless black crust at the chigger bite site) with regional lymphadenopathy, fever and a truncal rash in a rural or plantation worker is classic scrub typhus, caused by Orientia tsutsugamushi. Eschars hide in the groin, axilla and waistband, so the whole body must be examined. Murine typhus has no eschar.
w: Wrong - leptospirosis causes fever, myalgia (calves) and conjunctival suffusion but no eschar.
Correct - an eschar with regional nodes and fever in a plantation worker is scrub typhus.
Wrong - murine typhus is flea-borne, usually urban, and does not produce an eschar.
Wrong - dengue causes fever, myalgia and rash but not an eschar or lymphadenopathy.
Wrong - typhoid causes step-ladder fever, abdominal symptoms and rose spots, not an eschar.

mcq.stem:
A 70 kg man with fever for 6 days has an eschar on his waistline and a maculopapular truncal rash after clearing scrub in a rubber estate. He is not allergic to any drug. You plan to start treatment before transferring him to hospital.
Which antibiotic regimen is first-line?
o: Oral amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily
Oral cloxacillin 500 mg four times daily
mcq.e: Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7–10 days is first-line for all rickettsial infections, including scrub typhus; fever usually settles within 24–48 hours. Beta-lactams do not act on intracellular Orientia. The slides advise referring all typhus cases to hospital, but treatment should not be delayed for serology.
w: Wrong - beta-lactams are ineffective against intracellular rickettsiae.
Wrong - fluoroquinolones are not first-line for scrub typhus and treatment failures occur.
Wrong - cloxacillin targets staphylococci and has no rickettsial activity.
Correct - doxycycline 100 mg twice daily is first-line for scrub typhus.
Wrong - cephalosporins do not treat rickettsial infection.

mcq.stem:
A 6-year-old boy weighing 20 kg from an Orang Asli settlement has fever for 7 days, an eschar behind his knee and a truncal rash. His mother is worried that the medicine will stain his teeth.
What is the most appropriate treatment?
mcq.e: Doxycycline is the drug of choice for suspected rickettsial disease at any age, including children under 8 years; children under 45 kg receive 2.2 mg/kg twice daily (44 mg here). Short courses carry minimal risk of dental staining, unlike older tetracyclines, whereas delayed treatment causes serious complications.
w: Correct - doxycycline 2.2 mg/kg twice daily is first-line in children; short courses rarely stain teeth.
Wrong - amoxicillin does not treat rickettsial infection.
Wrong - cefuroxime has no activity against Orientia tsutsugamushi.
Wrong - cloxacillin is an anti-staphylococcal penicillin and ineffective here.
Wrong - treatment must not wait for serology when the clinical picture is typical.

mcq.stem:
A 38-year-old jungle trekker is investigated for prolonged fever with lymphadenopathy. Several serology results come back from the state laboratory.
Which result meets the MOH laboratory criterion for scrub typhus?
o: Two-fold rise in titre in paired sera
mcq.e: The MOH case definition requires an immunoperoxidase IgG titre of 1:400 or more, an IgM titre of 1:50 or more, or a four-fold rise in titre in paired sera (or isolation of the organism). Weil-Felix is cheap but has poor sensitivity and specificity, so it is not a laboratory criterion.
w: Wrong - Weil-Felix is only supportive and is not part of the case definition.
Wrong - an IgG of 1:200 is below the 1:400 threshold.
Wrong - an IgM of 1:25 is below the 1:50 threshold.
Correct - an IgG titre of 1:800 exceeds the 1:400 criterion.
Wrong - a four-fold rise in paired sera is required, not two-fold.

mcq.stem:
A 30-year-old warehouse worker at Port Klang, where rats are commonly seen, has fever, headache, myalgia and a dry cough for 8 days. A maculopapular rash is present over the axillae, the inner surfaces of the arms and the trunk. A careful search finds no eschar.
Which organism is most likely?
mcq.e: Murine typhus is caused by Rickettsia typhi, spread by rat and cat fleas, often in urban or port areas, with a rash over the axillae, inner arms and trunk and a non-productive cough. Scrub typhus (Orientia) usually produces an eschar, and epidemic typhus (R. prowazekii) is louse-borne in overcrowded settings.
w: Correct - flea-borne R. typhi causes murine typhus in rat-infested urban and port settings, without an eschar.
Wrong - Orientia causes scrub typhus after chigger bites in rural areas and typically leaves an eschar.
Wrong - R. prowazekii is louse-borne and occurs with extreme overcrowding such as refugee camps.
Wrong - leptospirosis is rat-associated but does not typically cause this truncal and axillary rash.
Wrong - typhoid causes rose spots on the abdomen with abdominal symptoms.

mcq.stem:
A 24-year-old man has had fever for 9 days, rising a little higher each day, with headache, anorexia, constipation and vague abdominal pain. Temperature 39.6°C, pulse 84/min. He has mild abdominal tenderness, a palpable spleen and a few faint salmon-pink blanching macules on the upper abdomen.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcq.e: Step-ladder prolonged fever, abdominal symptoms with constipation, splenomegaly, relative bradycardia (pulse 84 at 39.6°C) and rose spots on the abdomen are classic enteric fever. Dengue fever lasts 2–7 days, and scrub typhus would usually show an eschar.
w: Wrong - dengue fever usually lasts 2–7 days without step-ladder fever or splenomegaly.
Wrong - scrub typhus typically has an eschar with lymphadenopathy.
Correct - step-ladder fever, relative bradycardia, splenomegaly and rose spots indicate typhoid.
Wrong - leptospirosis causes abrupt fever, calf myalgia and conjunctival suffusion.
Wrong - hepatitis A causes jaundice and tender hepatomegaly, with fever settling as jaundice appears.

mcq.stem:
A 33-year-old woman has had fever for 5 days with headache and abdominal discomfort. She has taken no antibiotics. You suspect enteric fever.
Which investigation is the most appropriate first confirmatory test?
mcq.e: Blood culture gives its best yield in the first week of illness, before antibiotics, and is the standard confirmatory test. Bone marrow culture is the most sensitive but invasive and reserved for difficult cases. Stool culture becomes positive more often from weeks 2–3, and a single Widal titre is unreliable.
w: Wrong - Widal is unreliable, with false positives in endemic areas and false negatives early.
Wrong - stool culture is more often positive from the second or third week.
Wrong - urine culture has low yield in typhoid.
Wrong - bone marrow culture is the most sensitive but is invasive and not the first test.
Correct - blood culture before antibiotics is the first-line test in week 1.

mcq.stem:
A 28-year-old man with blood-culture-confirmed typhoid is clinically stable and able to take oral medication. Sensitivity results are pending. The physician plans oral treatment for uncomplicated disease.
Which empirical antibiotic is most appropriate, given resistance patterns in Asia?
mcq.e: Fluoroquinolone (ciprofloxacin) resistance is common in Salmonella Typhi isolates from Asia, so oral azithromycin is preferred for uncomplicated typhoid, and IV ceftriaxone for severe disease. Older first-line agents (amoxicillin, cotrimoxazole, chloramphenicol) are limited by multidrug resistance. Therapy is adjusted once sensitivities are known.
w: Wrong - reduced ciprofloxacin susceptibility is widespread in Asian isolates, so it is avoided empirically.
Correct - oral azithromycin is the preferred empirical oral agent for uncomplicated typhoid.
Wrong - amoxicillin is limited by multidrug resistance and is not used empirically.
Wrong - doxycycline is for rickettsial infection, not typhoid.
Wrong - cotrimoxazole is limited by multidrug resistance.

mcq.stem:
A 30-year-old woman completed treatment for culture-confirmed typhoid. Six weeks later she again develops fever and headache, and a blood culture grows Salmonella Typhi.
How should this episode be classified?
mcq.e: The MOH case classification defines relapse as recurrence of typhoid symptoms with a positive culture within 3 months, and reinfection as recurrence with a positive culture after more than 3 months. A chronic carrier is asymptomatic and excretes the organism for more than a year.
w: Wrong - reinfection is defined as a positive-culture recurrence more than 3 months later.
Correct - a culture-positive recurrence within 3 months is a relapse.
Wrong - a probable case is a suspected case with positive serology.
Wrong - a carrier is asymptomatic and excretes the organism for more than a year.
Wrong - a suspected case meets the clinical criteria only, without laboratory evidence.

mcq.stem:
A 40-year-old woman who runs a nasi lemak stall has recovered from culture-confirmed typhoid and finished her antibiotics. She is well and anxious to reopen her stall. The district health office is following her up.
When can she return to handling food?
o: Once she has completed the full antibiotic course
After a single negative stool culture
After two symptom-free weeks at home
After a negative Widal test on review
mcq.e: Food handlers are the commonest source of typhoid and may become carriers, usually from the gallbladder. They must not handle food until cleared by three consecutive negative stool cultures, with further follow-up cultures. Feeling well or finishing antibiotics does not prove clearance.
w: Wrong - finishing antibiotics does not exclude ongoing faecal excretion.
Wrong - shedding is intermittent, so a single negative culture is insufficient.
Wrong - being symptom-free does not exclude carriage.
Wrong - Widal does not detect carriage and is unreliable.
Correct - clearance requires three consecutive negative stool cultures before returning to food handling.

mcq.stem:
A 22-year-old man in the third week of untreated enteric fever develops sudden severe abdominal pain. He is pale and sweaty, pulse 128/min, BP 90/60 mmHg, with a rigid, silent abdomen.
What is the most likely complication?
mcq.e: Intestinal perforation and haemorrhage typically occur in the third week of typhoid, when the inflamed Peyer patches of the terminal ileum ulcerate. Sudden pain with peritonism and shock needs resuscitation and an urgent surgical referral.
w: Wrong - cholecystitis causes right upper quadrant pain, not generalised peritonitis with a silent abdomen.
Wrong - typhoid hepatitis causes tender hepatomegaly and jaundice, not a rigid abdomen.
Wrong - pancreatitis is an uncommon complication and gives epigastric pain radiating to the back.
Correct - perforation of ulcerated Peyer patches in the third week causes peritonitis and shock.
Wrong - mesenteric adenitis causes milder right iliac fossa pain without peritonism or shock.

mcq.stem:
A 35-year-old food handler attends a Klinik Kesihatan for mandatory typhoid vaccination. He prefers a single injection rather than tablets.
Which vaccine schedule is correct?
o: Vi polysaccharide, single IM dose, booster every 3 years
Ty21a, single IM dose, booster every 3 years
Vi polysaccharide, 3 oral doses, booster every 10 years
Ty21a, 3 oral doses, no booster needed
Vi polysaccharide, single IM dose, lifelong protection
mcq.e: The injectable Vi capsular polysaccharide vaccine is a single IM dose, while oral live attenuated Ty21a is given as 3 doses 2 days apart. Food handlers in Malaysia need a booster every 3 years because protection wanes. Ty21a is live and avoided in pregnancy and immunosuppression.
w: Correct - Vi polysaccharide is a single IM dose, with boosters every 3 years for food handlers.
Wrong - Ty21a is an oral live vaccine, not an injection.
Wrong - Vi polysaccharide is injected, not taken orally.
Wrong - Ty21a is not injectable and food handlers do need boosters.
Wrong - protection wanes, so boosters every 3 years are required.

mcq.stem:
A 7-year-old girl has had fever and a painful sore throat for 2 days. She has a fine, red rash on her neck and trunk that feels rough to touch, accentuated in the antecubital fossae. Her cheeks are flushed with pallor around the mouth, and her tonsils are swollen with white exudate. There is no conjunctivitis.
Which organism is most likely responsible?
mcq.e: Scarlet fever is caused by toxin-producing group A Streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes), usually with pharyngitis in children aged 5–15 years. The sandpaper rash, Pastia lines in skin creases and circumoral pallor are characteristic. EBV causes exudative tonsillitis but not this rash, except after amoxicillin.
w: Wrong - Staphylococcus aureus causes toxic shock syndrome or scalded skin syndrome, not exudative tonsillitis with a sandpaper rash.
Wrong - EBV causes exudative tonsillitis but not a sandpaper rash with Pastia lines.
Correct - group A Streptococcus pharyngitis with an erythrogenic toxin causes scarlet fever.
Wrong - HHV-6 causes roseola in infants, with a rash after the fever settles.
Wrong - measles has the 3 Cs and Koplik spots with a blotchy maculopapular rash.

mcq.stem:
An 8-year-old boy weighing 25 kg has exudative tonsillitis, a sandpaper rash and a strawberry tongue. A rapid streptococcal antigen test is positive. He has no drug allergies and is drinking adequately.
What is the most appropriate treatment?
mcq.e: Group A streptococcal pharyngitis and scarlet fever are treated with phenoxymethylpenicillin (or amoxicillin) for a full 10 days to eradicate the organism from the pharynx and prevent acute rheumatic fever. Erythromycin or another macrolide is used if he is allergic to penicillin.
w: Correct - a 10-day course of penicillin V eradicates GAS and prevents rheumatic fever.
Wrong - 5 days is too short to reliably eradicate pharyngeal GAS.
Wrong - cloxacillin is anti-staphylococcal and is not first-line for GAS.
Wrong - ciprofloxacin has poor streptococcal activity and is not used in children for this.
Wrong - antibiotics are needed to prevent complications and reduce spread.

mcq.stem:
A mother brings her 9-year-old daughter, who is on day 3 of penicillin V for scarlet fever. The fever has gone and the girl feels well. The mother wants to stop the medicine to avoid 'too many antibiotics'.
What is the main reason to complete the full 10-day course?
o: To stop the rash from coming back
To prevent penicillin resistance in GAS
mcq.e: A full 10-day course eradicates group A Streptococcus from the pharynx and prevents acute rheumatic fever if started within 9 days of onset. Antibiotics do not reliably prevent post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, which is the trap. Infectivity is already low after 24 hours of antibiotics.
w: Wrong - antibiotic treatment does not reliably prevent post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.
Wrong - the rash fades and peels regardless; preventing its recurrence is not the reason.
Correct - completing 10 days eradicates GAS and prevents acute rheumatic fever.
Wrong - GAS remains universally penicillin-sensitive.
Wrong - infectivity falls within 24 hours of starting antibiotics; the long course is for eradication.

mcq.stem:
A 9-year-old boy had a sore throat and a rough red rash 2 weeks ago that was not treated. He now has puffy eyes in the mornings, reduced urine output and cola-coloured urine. BP 130/85 mmHg. Urine dipstick shows blood 3+ and protein 1+.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcq.e: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis follows group A streptococcal pharyngitis by about 1–3 weeks, causing haematuria, oedema, hypertension and oliguria. IgA nephropathy causes haematuria within 1–2 days of an upper respiratory infection (synpharyngitic). An ASO titre and low C3 support the diagnosis.
w: Wrong - rheumatic fever presents with arthritis, carditis or chorea 2–4 weeks after GAS pharyngitis, not nephritis.
Wrong - IgA nephropathy causes haematuria at the same time as the throat infection, not 2 weeks later.
Wrong - HUS follows bloody diarrhoea, with haemolytic anaemia and thrombocytopenia.
Wrong - nephrotic syndrome causes heavy proteinuria and oedema without marked haematuria or hypertension.
Correct - nephritic syndrome 1–3 weeks after streptococcal pharyngitis is post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.

mcq.stem:
A 6-year-old boy started amoxicillin for scarlet fever yesterday afternoon. Today, after 24 hours of treatment, he is afebrile and eating. His parents both work and ask when he can return to school.
What is the correct advice?
o: Only after the full 10-day course is complete
After 24 hours of antibiotics if he is improving
Once the skin has finished peeling
After a negative repeat throat swab
Once he has been afebrile for 48 hours
mcq.e: Children with scarlet fever may return to school or daycare after completing 24 hours of antibiotics, provided they are clinically improving, because infectivity falls rapidly with treatment. Skin peeling can continue for weeks and is not infectious. Hand and environmental hygiene should be reinforced.
w: Wrong - he does not need to finish the course before returning; infectivity falls within 24 hours.
Correct - return is allowed after 24 hours of antibiotics if he is clinically improving.
Wrong - desquamation can last weeks and is not a marker of infectivity.
Wrong - a test of cure is not required for return to school.
Wrong - the criterion is 24 hours of antibiotics plus clinical improvement, not 48 hours without fever.

mcq.stem:
A 22-year-old woman on day 3 of her period, using tampons, presents with sudden high fever (39.8°C), vomiting, watery diarrhoea and confusion. She has a diffuse, blanching, sunburn-like erythema over her trunk and limbs. BP 80/50 mmHg, pulse 130/min. There is no petechial rash or neck stiffness.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcq.e: Toxic shock syndrome is a toxin-mediated illness, usually from Staphylococcus aureus, with sudden high fever, a diffuse sunburn-like erythroderma, hypotension and multi-organ involvement (GI, CNS). Tampon use, nasal packing and wound infection are classic risk factors, and desquamation follows 1–2 weeks later.
w: Wrong - meningococcaemia typically has a non-blanching petechial or purpuric rash.
Wrong - scarlet fever has a sandpaper rash with pharyngitis and rarely causes shock.
Wrong - SJS causes painful dusky macules, blisters and mucosal erosions after a drug.
Correct - tampon use with fever, sunburn-like rash, hypotension and GI and CNS involvement is toxic shock syndrome.
Wrong - dengue shock occurs at defervescence after several days of fever, not with an erythroderma.

mcq.stem:
A 19-year-old woman is brought to a Klinik Kesihatan on day 4 of her menstrual period. She has had sudden fever, vomiting and diarrhoea since this morning and is now drowsy. She has a diffuse, blanching, sunburn-like erythema. Temperature 40.1°C, BP 78/40 mmHg, pulse 138/min, SpO2 95% on room air. She confirms she is still wearing a tampon. Oxygen is started and two large-bore IV cannulae are inserted.
What is the best next step?
o: Start oral cloxacillin and review her in clinic within 24 hours
Give IM hydrocortisone and promethazine, then observe for 2 hours
Remove the tampon, give an IV crystalloid bolus and transfer urgently
Send blood cultures and FBC and start antibiotics once results return
Give oral paracetamol and refer to the dermatology clinic tomorrow
mcq.e: Suspected toxic shock syndrome is an emergency: stabilise ABC with oxygen and IV fluids, remove the toxin source (tampon, nasal or wound packing) and arrange urgent hospital transfer with empirical antibiotics. Leaving the tampon in place allows continued toxin production. Antibiotics must never wait for laboratory results in a shocked patient.
w: Wrong - oral antibiotics and outpatient review are unsafe in a hypotensive, drowsy patient.
Wrong - this treats anaphylaxis; the picture of fever, shock and erythroderma with a tampon is toxin-mediated, not allergic.
Correct - source removal, fluid resuscitation and urgent transfer are the key primary-care actions in toxic shock.
Wrong - cultures are useful but antibiotics must not be delayed for results in septic shock.
Wrong - this misreads the rash as a skin problem and ignores life-threatening shock.

mcq.stem:
A 34-year-old man is seen at a health clinic 4 days after a nasal fracture was treated with nasal packing. He has fever 39.6°C, vomiting, myalgia, confusion and a diffuse macular erythroderma including the palms. BP 82/50 mmHg after a 1 L saline bolus. The packing has been removed and an ambulance is on its way.
Which empirical antibiotic combination is most appropriate to start now?
mcq.e: Empirical therapy for toxic shock syndrome combines a broad-spectrum beta-lactam (ceftriaxone) with clindamycin. Clindamycin inhibits bacterial protein synthesis and so switches off toxin production, and it still works when the bacterial load is high and organisms are not dividing. Doxycycline is the drug for rickettsial illness, not toxin-mediated staphylococcal or streptococcal shock.
w: Correct - a beta-lactam plus clindamycin covers S. aureus and group A streptococcus and suppresses toxin production.
Wrong - doxycycline targets rickettsiae (scrub typhus) and does not suppress staphylococcal toxin.
Wrong - this covers anaerobes and gut flora, and amoxicillin does not cover most S. aureus.
Wrong - gentamicin is not used for toxin suppression, and penicillin alone misses most S. aureus.
Wrong - this combination is not a recommended regimen for toxic shock syndrome.

mcq.stem:
A 24-year-old woman attends a Klinik Kesihatan 11 days after admission for tampon-associated toxic shock syndrome. She completed IV antibiotics and feels well. She is worried because the skin of her palms and soles is now peeling in large sheets. She is afebrile, BP 116/72 mmHg, with no mucosal lesions, no blisters elsewhere and no pain.
What is the most likely explanation for the peeling?
o: Stevens-Johnson syndrome caused by her clindamycin
Recurrent toxic shock syndrome needing readmission
Contact dermatitis from hospital antiseptic washes
Hand eczema triggered by repeated alcohol hand rub
Normal late desquamation after the toxin rash
mcq.e: Desquamation of the palms and soles typically appears 1–2 weeks after the acute illness in toxic shock syndrome and is part of the expected course, not a new disease. A well, afebrile patient with painless peeling and no mucosal involvement needs reassurance plus advice to avoid tampons because TSS can recur.
w: Wrong - SJS is painful, starts with dusky target lesions and involves mucosa; she is well with painless peeling.
Wrong - recurrence would bring back fever, rash and hypotension; she is afebrile and normotensive.
Wrong - contact dermatitis is itchy and inflamed at the contact site rather than sheet-like acral peeling.
Wrong - eczema is itchy and fissured and does not involve the soles after a single admission.
Correct - palm and sole desquamation 1–2 weeks after onset is the classic late sign of toxic shock syndrome.

mcq.stem:
A 17-year-old boarding-school student is brought to a Klinik Kesihatan with fever for 6 hours, headache, leg pains and cold hands. There are several purple spots on his thighs that do not fade under a pressed glass. Temperature 39.4°C, pulse 124/min, BP 100/60 mmHg, CRT 3 seconds. The hospital is 40 minutes away by ambulance.
What is the most appropriate immediate action?
o: Take blood cultures first, then refer to hospital by ambulance
Give benzylpenicillin 2.4 g IV or IM now, then transfer urgently
Check FBC for platelets before deciding whether to give antibiotics
Give oral amoxicillin 1 g stat and review him again in 6 hours
Arrange lumbar puncture in hospital before any antibiotic is given
mcq.e: Fever with a non-blanching rash is meningococcal septicaemia until proven otherwise, and the slides stress that treatment is extremely urgent and should be given before reaching hospital. Benzylpenicillin 2.4 g IV/IM (or ceftriaxone 2 g) is given in the clinic, then the patient is transferred. Investigations, including cultures and lumbar puncture, must never delay the first dose.
w: Wrong - a delay to obtain cultures is not justified; give antibiotics first if cultures cannot be taken immediately.
Correct - pre-hospital parenteral benzylpenicillin followed by urgent transfer saves lives in meningococcaemia.
Wrong - a platelet count does not change the decision and wastes time in a rapidly progressive illness.
Wrong - oral antibiotics and delayed review are dangerous in suspected meningococcal sepsis.
Wrong - lumbar puncture is contraindicated in septic shock and must never delay antibiotics.

mcq.stem:
A 4-year-old boy weighing 16 kg is seen at a rural Klinik Kesihatan with fever for 8 hours, lethargy, cold peripheries and a spreading non-blanching purpuric rash on his legs. He has no drug allergies. IM benzylpenicillin is to be given before the ambulance transfer.
What is the correct dose?
mcq.e: The pre-hospital benzylpenicillin dose for a child is 60 mg/kg, to a maximum of 2.4 g. For 16 kg this is 16 × 60 = 960 mg. Under-dosing loses precious bactericidal effect, while the adult dose of 2.4 g is only reached at 40 kg.
w: Wrong - 240 mg is only 15 mg/kg, a quarter of the required dose.
Wrong - 480 mg is 30 mg/kg, half the required dose.
Wrong - 2400 mg is the adult maximum and is reached only at 40 kg body weight.
Correct - 60 mg/kg × 16 kg = 960 mg, below the 2.4 g ceiling.
Wrong - 1600 mg is 100 mg/kg, well above the recommended weight-based dose.

mcq.stem:
A 25-year-old woman shares a flat with a colleague admitted yesterday with confirmed meningococcal septicaemia. She is well. She takes a combined oral contraceptive pill and wears soft contact lenses. You prescribe rifampicin 600 mg twice daily for 2 days as chemoprophylaxis.
Which counselling point is most important for her?
o: Take it with milk to reduce the risk of tendon rupture
Avoid sunlight for 2 weeks because of photosensitivity
Stop the pill for a month because rifampicin raises oestrogen
Use condoms too; rifampicin makes the pill less reliable
Expect a metallic taste and avoid all alcohol for 48 hours
mcq.e: Rifampicin is a potent liver enzyme inducer that lowers oestrogen and progestogen levels, so combined pill users need additional barrier contraception during the course and for 4 weeks afterwards. She should also be warned that urine, tears and sweat turn orange-red and may stain soft contact lenses. The distractors describe side effects of quinolones, doxycycline and metronidazole.
w: Wrong - tendon rupture is a fluoroquinolone (ciprofloxacin) warning, not rifampicin.
Wrong - photosensitivity is the key warning for doxycycline.
Wrong - rifampicin lowers, not raises, hormone levels; stopping the pill leaves her unprotected.
Correct - enzyme induction reduces contraceptive efficacy, so extra barrier protection is needed.
Wrong - metallic taste and the alcohol reaction belong to metronidazole.

mcq.stem:
A 2-year-old girl is brought to a health clinic with fever for 7 hours. She cries when her legs are touched and refuses to walk. Her hands and feet are cold and her skin looks mottled. Temperature 39.2°C, heart rate 180/min, CRT 4 seconds. There is a single 2 mm non-blanching spot on her ankle. No cough, no diarrhoea.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcq.e: Leg pain, cold hands and feet and abnormal skin colour are early signs of meningococcal sepsis that often appear within the first hours, before the classic purpuric rash spreads. Tachycardia with prolonged CRT means compensated shock. Even a single non-blanching spot in a febrile, unwell child demands immediate parenteral antibiotics and transfer.
w: Correct - early leg pain, cold peripheries, mottling and shock with a non-blanching spot are meningococcal sepsis.
Wrong - dengue shock occurs at defervescence (around day 3–7), not 7 hours into the fever.
Wrong - viral myositis does not cause shock, mottling or a non-blanching rash.
Wrong - HSP gives palpable purpura on buttocks and legs in a usually well, normotensive child.
Wrong - reactive arthritis follows an infection by weeks and does not cause shock.

mcq.stem:
A 45-year-old man with well-controlled hypertension visits a Klinik Kesihatan to prepare for Umrah in 6 weeks. He received no vaccines as an adult. He asks which vaccine Saudi Arabia requires for pilgrims.
Which vaccine is mandatory?
mcq.e: Saudi Arabia requires proof of quadrivalent meningococcal ACWY vaccination for Hajj and Umrah pilgrims, given at least 10 days before arrival. MenB and MenACWY are separate vaccines covering different serogroups, so MenB does not satisfy the requirement. Yellow fever is required only for travellers from endemic countries.
w: Wrong - MenB covers serogroup B only and is not the pilgrimage requirement.
Wrong - typhoid vaccine is advisable for some travellers but is not mandatory for Umrah.
Correct - MenACWY is the mandatory vaccine for Hajj and Umrah pilgrims.
Wrong - MenC alone misses serogroups A, W and Y, which caused Hajj-related outbreaks.
Wrong - yellow fever is required only for travellers from endemic countries, not Malaysia.

mcq.stem:
A 20-year-old university student was admitted last night with confirmed meningococcal septicaemia. The district health office asks you to identify contacts at a Klinik Kesihatan. Several people are worried and attend today; all are well.
Which person most clearly needs antibiotic chemoprophylaxis?
o: The ambulance driver who transported him to hospital
The clinic nurse who measured his blood pressure
A classmate who sat across the lecture hall from him
A colleague who met him briefly in an office last week
His girlfriend, who kissed him 2 days before onset
mcq.e: Chemoprophylaxis is for close contacts with prolonged or intimate exposure to oral secretions in the 7 days before illness onset: household and dormitory contacts and kissing contacts. Casual contacts and most healthcare workers do not need it unless directly exposed to respiratory secretions (for example during intubation without a mask). Give it as soon as possible, ideally within 24 hours.
w: Wrong - transporting a patient is casual contact without secretion exposure.
Wrong - routine examination is not an indication; only direct airway secretion exposure is.
Wrong - sitting in the same lecture hall is casual contact.
Wrong - a brief meeting is casual contact and carries no significant risk.
Correct - kissing contacts in the 7 days before onset are close contacts needing prophylaxis.

mcq.stem:
A 32-year-old man attends a Klinik Kesihatan. He started carbamazepine from a private clinic 3 weeks ago for trigeminal neuralgia. Two days of fever, sore throat and malaise were followed by painful dusky red macules with dark centres on his trunk, erosions of the lips and mouth, and red eyes. Gentle lateral pressure shears off the epidermis. Detached skin is estimated at about 5% of body surface area.
Which diagnosis best fits?
mcq.e: Drug exposure 1–4 weeks earlier, a flu-like prodrome, painful dusky macules, mucosal erosions at two or more sites and a positive Nikolsky sign indicate epidermal necrolysis. Classification is by detached body surface area: SJS below 10%, overlap 10–30% and TEN above 30%. Erythema multiforme major has typical raised acral targets, is usually HSV-triggered and lacks widespread detachment.
w: Wrong - EM major has typical acral target lesions, usually follows HSV and does not cause Nikolsky-positive detachment.
Correct - a drug-triggered mucocutaneous reaction with detachment under 10% BSA is SJS.
Wrong - overlap requires 10–30% BSA detachment.
Wrong - TEN requires more than 30% BSA detachment.
Wrong - SSSS affects young children, spares mucosa and is toxin-mediated, not drug-induced.

mcq.stem:
A 58-year-old man with gout was started on allopurinol 300 mg daily 2 weeks ago. He presents to a Klinik Kesihatan with 2 days of fever and sore throat, followed by painful dusky macules with blistering on his chest, oral erosions and gritty red eyes. Nikolsky sign is positive. Temperature 38.6°C, BP 118/76 mmHg, pulse 104/min.
What is the best next step?
o: Continue allopurinol, add oral prednisolone and review in 3 days
Stop allopurinol at once and refer urgently to hospital
Keep allopurinol until a skin biopsy confirms the diagnosis
Switch allopurinol to febuxostat and give oral cetirizine
Give IM chlorpheniramine and discharge with calamine lotion
mcq.e: In suspected SJS/TEN the single most important step is to stop the suspected drug immediately, then refer urgently for supportive care in hospital (ICU or burns unit with dermatology and ophthalmology input). Delay in withdrawing the culprit worsens prognosis. Investigations such as skin biopsy must not delay referral, and antihistamines or calamine treat urticaria, not epidermal necrolysis.
w: Wrong - continuing the culprit drug allows the reaction to progress; steroids do not replace drug withdrawal.
Correct - immediate withdrawal of the culprit and urgent hospital referral are the key steps.
Wrong - biopsy confirms full-thickness necrosis but must never delay stopping the drug or referral.
Wrong - starting a new urate-lowering drug during an acute reaction is inappropriate, and antihistamines do not help.
Wrong - this treats a mild allergic rash and dangerously underestimates a mucocutaneous emergency.

mcq.stem:
A 26-year-old woman of Chinese ethnicity has newly diagnosed focal epilepsy. The neurologist plans to start carbamazepine and she visits a Klinik Kesihatan for pre-treatment blood tests. She has no drug allergies.
Which test is most important before the first dose to prevent a severe cutaneous reaction?
mcq.e: HLA-B*1502 is strongly associated with carbamazepine-induced SJS/TEN in Asian populations, including Han Chinese and Malays, so screening is recommended before starting carbamazepine; carriers should receive an alternative drug. HLA-B*5801 is the allele linked to allopurinol reactions. Patch testing is not a reliable predictor before first exposure.
w: Wrong - a drug level is meaningless before the drug is started and does not predict hypersensitivity.
Wrong - liver tests are reasonable baseline monitoring but do not predict SJS risk.
Wrong - HLA-B*5801 predicts allopurinol hypersensitivity, not carbamazepine.
Correct - HLA-B*1502 carriers have a high risk of carbamazepine-induced SJS/TEN.
Wrong - patch testing is not validated to predict SJS risk before the drug is ever taken.

mcq.stem:
A 9-year-old boy has had a dry cough and low-grade fever for 8 days; his chest X-ray shows patchy bilateral infiltrates. Over 2 days he has developed severe painful erosions of the lips and mouth, bilateral conjunctivitis and a few target-like lesions on his trunk. He has taken only paracetamol. There are no vesicles on the hands or feet and no Koplik spots.
What is the most likely trigger of his mucocutaneous reaction?
mcq.e: Besides drugs, infections can trigger SJS, and Mycoplasma pneumoniae is the commonest infective trigger in children, followed by HSV. An atypical pneumonia with dry cough and infiltrates followed by prominent mucositis and sparse skin lesions is the typical pattern. HFMD causes oral ulcers with hand and foot vesicles, and measles causes conjunctivitis with Koplik spots and a descending rash.
w: Correct - Mycoplasma atypical pneumonia is the leading infective trigger of SJS in children.
Wrong - group A streptococcus causes scarlet fever and pharyngitis, not mucositis with atypical pneumonia.
Wrong - S. aureus causes toxin-mediated SSSS or TSS without severe mucosal erosions.
Wrong - measles gives coryza, Koplik spots and a descending maculopapular rash.
Wrong - coxsackie A16 causes HFMD with hand and foot vesicles, which are absent here.

mcq.stem:
A 40-year-old woman is diagnosed at a Klinik Kesihatan with a cotrimoxazole-induced mucocutaneous reaction: dusky target lesions with blistering on 6% of body surface area, oral erosions and bilateral red, painful eyes with discharge and photophobia. The drug has been stopped and an ambulance is arranged.
Which specialist assessment should the referral letter request most urgently?
o: Dermatology patch testing to confirm the drug
Skin biopsy to be done before she is admitted
HLA-B*1502 genotyping to guide future drugs
Rheumatology review for an autoimmune screen
Ophthalmology assessment of the eye involvement
mcq.e: Ocular involvement in SJS/TEN can lead to corneal scarring, symblepharon and blindness, so urgent ophthalmology assessment is needed whenever the eyes are involved. Patch testing is done only after recovery, and biopsy must not delay referral. Genetic testing does not change acute management.
w: Wrong - patch testing is a post-recovery tool and has no role in the acute phase.
Wrong - biopsy is done in hospital and must never delay transfer.
Wrong - HLA testing is a pre-prescribing screen for carbamazepine, not acute care.
Wrong - an autoimmune screen does not address the threat to her vision.
Correct - eye involvement needs urgent ophthalmology input to prevent scarring and blindness.

mcq.stem:
A 3-year-old boy is seen at a Klinik Kesihatan with fever for 6 days despite paracetamol. He is very irritable. He has bilateral non-purulent conjunctival injection sparing the limbus, red cracked lips with a red bumpy tongue, a polymorphous rash on the trunk and swollen, red hands and feet. No cough or coryza, no Koplik spots. A rapid strep test is negative.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcq.e: Fever for 5 days or more with at least 4 of the 5 CRASH features (Conjunctivitis, Rash, Adenopathy, Strawberry tongue and mucosal changes, Hand and foot changes) meets the criteria for Kawasaki disease; this child has 4. The look-alikes are excluded by the absence of coryza and Koplik spots (measles), a negative strep test (scarlet fever) and normal blood pressure (TSS). Note: the slide writes fever >5 days; the standard criterion is 5 days or more.
w: Wrong - measles has cough, coryza, Koplik spots and a rash starting behind the ears.
Wrong - scarlet fever shows a sandpaper rash with exudative pharyngitis and a positive strep test.
Correct - 6 days of fever plus 4 CRASH features is classic Kawasaki disease.
Wrong - adenovirus gives exudative conjunctivitis and pharyngitis but not hand and foot changes.
Wrong - TSS presents with hypotension and erythroderma, and he is not shocked.

mcq.stem:
An 8-month-old girl is brought to a health clinic with fever for 7 days and marked irritability. She has bilateral non-purulent conjunctival injection and a faint maculopapular rash, but no lip, hand, foot or lymph node changes. Blood tests: WBC 18 × 10⁹/L, platelets 560 × 10⁹/L, CRP 110 mg/L, albumin 28 g/L; urine microscopy shows sterile pyuria.
What is the best next step?
o: Refer urgently to paediatrics for assessment and echocardiogram
Reassure the mother, as she does not meet 4 of the 5 criteria
Treat the pyuria as a UTI with oral cefuroxime for 7 days
Repeat the FBC and CRP at the clinic in 1 week to see the trend
Start high-dose oral aspirin at the clinic and review in 2 days
mcq.e: Incomplete Kawasaki disease, with fewer than 4 principal features, is most common in infants under 12 months, who also have the highest risk of coronary aneurysm. Unexplained prolonged fever with raised inflammatory markers, thrombocytosis, low albumin and sterile pyuria should prompt urgent paediatric referral with a low threshold for echocardiography. Delayed diagnosis leads to late IVIG and more coronary complications.
w: Correct - suspected incomplete KD in an infant needs urgent paediatric review and echocardiography.
Wrong - infants often have incomplete KD; failing to meet 4 criteria does not exclude it.
Wrong - sterile pyuria is a known feature of KD, and treating it as UTI delays the diagnosis.
Wrong - waiting a week risks missing the window for IVIG and coronary protection.
Wrong - aspirin is started alongside IVIG in hospital after diagnosis, not alone at the clinic.

mcq.stem:
A 4-year-old boy weighing 18 kg is admitted on day 6 of fever and meets the criteria for classic Kawasaki disease. His first echocardiogram shows no coronary abnormality. The ward medical officer asks for the first-line regimen according to the Paediatric Protocols for Malaysian Hospitals.
Which regimen is correct?
o: IVIG 400 mg/kg daily for 5 days plus aspirin 3–5 mg/kg/day
Oral prednisolone 2 mg/kg/day alone, with aspirin avoided
IVIG 2 g/kg over 10–12 hours plus aspirin 30–50 mg/kg/day
IVIG 2 g/kg over 10–12 hours plus ibuprofen 10 mg/kg tds
IV methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg plus aspirin 3–5 mg/kg/day
mcq.e: First-line treatment is a single IVIG infusion of 2 g/kg over 10–12 hours, ideally within 10 days of onset, together with anti-inflammatory aspirin 30–50 mg/kg/day in divided doses. Kawasaki disease is the key exception to the rule of avoiding aspirin in children. Ibuprofen should be avoided because it blocks aspirin’s antiplatelet effect, and steroids are reserved for IVIG resistance.
w: Wrong - divided 5-day IVIG is not the standard regimen, and 3–5 mg/kg/day is the later antiplatelet dose.
Wrong - steroids are not first line and aspirin is specifically indicated in KD.
Correct - single-dose IVIG 2 g/kg plus high-dose aspirin is first-line therapy.
Wrong - ibuprofen antagonises aspirin’s antiplatelet effect and is not part of KD treatment.
Wrong - pulsed steroids are reserved for IVIG-resistant disease, not first-line use.

mcq.stem:
A 2-year-old girl with Kawasaki disease received IVIG 2 g/kg and has been on aspirin 40 mg/kg/day in divided doses. Her fever settled 3 days ago and she is now eating well. Her echocardiogram is normal.
When should her aspirin be reduced to the low antiplatelet dose of 3–5 mg/kg/day?
o: As soon as the IVIG infusion has finished
Only after a fixed 14-day course at high dose
Once the platelet count has fully normalised
After a normal echocardiogram at 6–8 weeks
At 48–72 hours after the fever has settled
mcq.e: Anti-inflammatory aspirin (30–50 mg/kg/day) is started with IVIG and reduced to antiplatelet aspirin (3–5 mg/kg/day) 48–72 hours after defervescence. The low dose then continues for 6–8 weeks or until ESR and platelets normalise, whichever is later, and indefinitely or until resolution if coronary lesions are present. Platelets rise in the subacute phase, so waiting for them to normalise would prolong high-dose exposure.
w: Wrong - the fever may persist after IVIG and high-dose aspirin is still needed for inflammation.
Wrong - the switch is guided by defervescence, not a fixed 14-day period.
Wrong - thrombocytosis peaks in the subacute phase; platelet normalisation guides stopping low-dose aspirin, not the switch.
Wrong - the 6–8 week echo guides stopping low-dose aspirin, not when to reduce the high dose.
Correct - aspirin is stepped down to 3–5 mg/kg/day 48–72 hours after defervescence.

mcq.stem:
A mother brings her 11-month-old son to a Klinik Kesihatan for his scheduled MMR dose next week. Six weeks ago he was treated in hospital for Kawasaki disease with IVIG 2 g/kg and aspirin; he is now well and his echo is normal. His other immunisations are up to date.
What is the most appropriate advice about his MMR vaccine?
o: Give the MMR vaccine next week as scheduled
Delay it 4 weeks, then give the MMR vaccine
Omit the MMR vaccine permanently after IVIG
Delay MMR until at least 11 months after IVIG
Give a double dose of MMR vaccine next week
mcq.e: High-dose IVIG contains antibodies that neutralise live attenuated viral vaccines such as MMR and varicella, so these should be delayed for at least 11 months after IVIG. Inactivated vaccines on the schedule can be given as normal. The child is not contraindicated permanently, and a larger dose does not overcome the passive antibody.
w: Wrong - IVIG antibodies would neutralise the live vaccine and the dose may fail.
Wrong - 4 weeks is far too short for passively acquired antibodies to wane after 2 g/kg IVIG.
Wrong - the vaccine is only postponed, not contraindicated permanently.
Correct - live vaccines are delayed for at least 11 months after high-dose IVIG.
Wrong - doubling the dose does not overcome passive antibody and is not recommended.

mcq.stem:
A 5-year-old boy is discharged after treatment for Kawasaki disease. His echocardiogram at diagnosis was normal. His mother asks the Klinik Kesihatan doctor whether more heart scans are needed, because he now seems completely well.
When should follow-up echocardiograms be done?
o: None are needed if the first echo was normal
At 2–3 weeks and 6–8 weeks after onset
Only if chest pain or breathlessness occur
Every month for a year, then once a year
At 6 months and 12 months after discharge
mcq.e: Coronary aneurysms usually develop in the subacute phase (2–4 weeks), so a normal echo at diagnosis does not exclude them. Transthoracic echocardiography is done at diagnosis, at 2–3 weeks and at 6–8 weeks after onset. Aneurysms are often silent until thrombosis causes myocardial infarction, so waiting for symptoms is unsafe.
w: Wrong - aneurysms form in the subacute phase and can be missed by the first echo.
Correct - the protocol repeats echo at 2–3 weeks and 6–8 weeks after onset.
Wrong - aneurysms are usually silent until thrombosis, so symptom-triggered scans are too late.
Wrong - monthly scans for a year are unnecessary when the scheduled echoes are normal.
Wrong - these timings miss the subacute window when aneurysms develop.
